A UK school estate was compromised by the 3AM ransomware group via a unique hybrid human-AI operation, an investigation by Bitdefender has found.

The incident, which took place from September 10 to 19, 2026, resulted in the attackers’ encrypting 37 machines and building domain trust in the compromised estate to reach other schools.

Notably, the investigation revealed that parts of the post-compromise techniques were undertaken by a human operator at the keyboard, while other parts behaved like an AI agent.

Bitdefender described the attack as “the first case of this kind that we have documented in Europe.”

The researchers continued: “What this attack does show is that the hybrid approach works, and we assess that it makes economic sense for attackers, with a person setting the goals and an [AI] model handling the mechanical work. We can expect hybrid attacks like this one to become more common in 2027.”

How 3AM’s Hybrid Attack Unfolded

The research blog, published on November 3, attributed the attack to a 3AM ransomware affiliate. 3AM is a ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation, whose Rust-based encryptor was first observed in February 2023.

The researchers were not able to determine how the attacker gained initial access to the school estate. The first recorded activity started on September 10, when the attackers’ accessed credentials stored the estate’s backup infrastructure, before decrypting them with the Windows Data Protection API.

From September 12-13, the threat actor tested connections to other hosts from a machine where SQL Server was the parent process. They sent a sequence of commands to the target’s Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) service, authenticating with stolen administrator credentials. The commands’ outputs were then read by either a person or AI model, who would then choose the next command and repeat the cycle.

A PowerShell command was first used, and re-ran unchanged 41 seconds later, before a single call was changed 49 seconds after that. Next, 47 seconds later, PowerShell was replaced with wmic, the older built-in command-line interface to WMI.

The researchers noted that the fact the complete rewrite arrived as fast as the minor changes before it indicates the commands were written by an AI agent.

The next nine retries followed a similar pattern of the delay before the next command being issued taking between 40 to 101 seconds, whatever the size of the change, while moving on to a new task to minutes.

“That split, longer time between tasks and shorter between retries, is what it looks like if a person is choosing the next step and a model is handling the retries,” the Bitdefender researchers wrote.

In contrast, later commands before the retry sequence were simpler and were sent between two and 16 minutes apart indicative of the pace of someone reading the output and deciding what to do next.

On September 14, the attacker made efforts to gain persistence in the compromised environments. These include running credential dumping tool Mimikatz and creating two backdoor domain-administrator accounts by separate routes.

Next, the attackers copied and 40 financial-related files via the Windows robocopy tool, which were subsequently exfiltrated to their command-and-control (C2) endpoint using HTTP POST.

“The registry-as-transport channel is an unusual choice and a strong indicator to hunt for,” the researchers noted.

On September 19, the attacker joined three separate Active Directory domains with two-way trusts and pushed the backdoor account’s access across the estate within an approximately three-hour window. The researchers said this part of the attack was the clearest example of the hybrid human-AI approach being deployed.

The work involved in joining the estate’s separate domains is highly mechanical, requiring it to be set up correctly on both sides, with one wrong detail stopping everything.

The attackers built the trusts and then ran a series of diagnostic probes and restarted the service that maintains the secure channel between domains. Bitdefender said the hybrid human-AI model suits this work, involving repetitive configuration where the fix comes from a human reading the error.

This work resulted in the attackers reaching 50 machines from the unmanaged host.

Finally, the threat actor made attempts to remove endpoint detection and response (EDR) tools, before decrypting 37 out of the 50 machines accessed.

How to Defend Against Hybrid AI Ransomware Attacks

Bitdefender noted that the attack involved typical approaches observed in other ransomware incidents, including backup credential theft, rogue domain administrators, trusts between domains and use of built-in legitimate tooling.

However, the hands-on work was split between human and AI operators, making use of their respective abilities.

“The approach looks pragmatic: the model takes the mechanical, repetitive work, and nothing in it needed skill or spend that these attackers did not already have,” the researchers commented.

They also noted that the involved of an AI model changes what the traces look like during an incident.

Bitdefender offered the following recommendations for defenders to protect against future attacks that follow a similar playbook:

Keep the administrative accounts of separate domains separate, and never keep privileged credentials for several domains in one place

Treat backup infrastructure as a target, and review your backup strategy for malicious intent

Restrict remote execution and administrative shares

Block interpreters and shells on machines that never use them

Put an endpoint agent on every machine

989fbcdc4378.text:
The developers of Goddess of Victory: NIKKE have confirmed that hackers tampered with the game's PC launcher scripts in a supply-chain attack, distributing malware capable of stealing credentials and cryptocurrency wallet data.

According to a notice published on X, a client update was issued on November 4 at 02:30 (UTC +9) to address the issue.

"We have identified an issue indicating that the PC Launcher's script files may have been tampered with by a third party," reads the statement on X.

"Accordingly, client fixes and an update were implemented on November 4 at approximately 02:30 (UTC+9). We are currently investigating the scope of the impact caused by this issue, and we will provide further details regarding follow-up measures in a separate notice."

Goddess of Victory: NIKKE is a popular sci-fi shooter RPG developed by the South Korean firm Shift Up for Windows, iOS, and Android.

Its publisher, Level Infinite, reported more than 45 million downloads since its launch in 2022, while Google Play alone reports 10 million downloads.

Malicious launcher scripts delivered backdoor

Although Level Infinite has not disclosed many details, a report on GitHub by independent security researcher MotherSphere alleges the incident involved four JavaScript files hosted on Level Infinite's official content delivery network (CDN).

According to the researcher, the files were modified on September 27, 2026, to inject malicious JavaScript that downloaded additional code from attacker-controlled servers whenever players opened the game launcher.

The injected code was hidden within legitimate JavaScript files and used obfuscation to conceal the domains insightjs[.]com and insightjs[.]org, from which the malicious code was downloaded.

BleepingComputer examined two of the modified JavaScript files and confirmed that they contained an obfuscated loader designed to retrieve and execute additional code from these domains, falling back to the second domain if the first was unavailable.

According to MotherSphere's analysis, the downloaded code abused the launcher's native functionality to retrieve and execute a malicious LuaJIT payload called insight.bundle, which installed a remote-access agent referred to as K2F.

The backdoor allowed attackers to remotely execute commands, browse and download local files, capture screenshots, collect NIKKE account credentials, and steal information stored in web browsers.

The malware also supported an additional command to install a malicious Windows DLL named platform_experience_helper.dll that could remain active after the game launcher was closed.

BleepingComputer analyzed strings extracted from a DLL sample uploaded to VirusTotal and found code indicating that the malware can steal cryptocurrency wallet data from browser extensions, including MetaMask, Phantom, Coinbase Wallet, and others.

The DLL contained functionality to intercept sensitive wallet information, including recovery phrases and private keys, potentially allowing attackers to steal cryptocurrency.

However, it is unknown whether the attackers deployed this additional component on infected systems or successfully stole cryptocurrency from players.

The researcher claims that Level Infinite replaced three of the impacted JavaScript files on November 3 with clean versions. However, they claim a tampered copy of the fourth was reportedly still being served to users as of 22:26 GMT.

This suggests that at least one compromised script may have remained accessible after the company deployed its client update.

The researcher also shared indicators of compromise (IOCs) that users can check to determine whether the malicious Lua agent executed on their computers.

One indicator is the string k2f_chan registered in the Launcher/intl_service/debug.log file within the NIKKE installation directory.

This entry indicates the malicious Lua agent executed, but it does not confirm whether the DLL was loaded as well.

BleepingComputer also found that the insightjs[.]org backup domain is now serving code that displays a security warning inside the game launcher.

The warning, displayed in English, Chinese, Japanese, and Korean, tells players to immediately close the launcher and refrain from opening the PC client until the publisher confirms the issue has been resolved.

The message confirms that this is not an official announcement from the game's publisher, so it unclear who currently controls the domain or when the malicious payload was replaced with the warning.

BleepingComputer has contacted Level Infinite for comment on MotherSphere's findings, but has not received a response by publication.

Potentially affected players should run a full system scan using updated antivirus software.

Those who find they were compromised should reinstall Windows, and change passwords and other sensitive credentials from a clean device.

CrowdStrike plans to acquire AI security companies Fiddler AI and Dreadnode in separate deals that will extend its Falcon platform into automated testing of AI systems and monitoring of AI agent behaviour, as enterprises look to address security risks arising from increasingly autonomous applications.

CrowdStrike made the announcements at Fal.Con Europe 2026 in Barcelona, saying the acquisitions will add capabilities to test AI models, applications, and agents for security weaknesses before deployment and monitor their decisions and actions in production.

The company plans to integrate Dreadnode’s automated testing technology and Fiddler’s agent observability capabilities into Falcon, with both offerings scheduled for general availability in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2027.

Dreadnode will bring automated security testing to identify vulnerabilities in AI models, applications and agents before deployment. Fiddler, meanwhile, will add AI agent observability and explainability, allowing enterprises to monitor agent behaviour, trace decisions and understand why agents take particular actions, CrowdStrike said in two separate statements.

CrowdStrike said the Dreadnode team will join its Cyber Superintelligence Lab, but did not specify how the Fiddler team would be integrated into the company.

CrowdStrike adds AI testing and observability

“With this acquisition, Dreadnode will extend the Falcon platform into the layer where enterprises build and test AI, delivering Automated AI Security Testing capabilities,” CrowdStrike said in its announcement.

It further added that Dreadnode’s technology will allow security teams to test AI models, applications, agent reasoning loops and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers against more than 100 AI attack strategies. These include jailbreaks, prompt injection, multi-turn attacks, and attacks targeting AI agents.

The technology will also let teams describe tests in natural language, rank findings by severity, and map vulnerabilities to frameworks including OWASP Top 10 for LLMs, OWASP Agentic Security, MITRE ATLAS, and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework. CrowdStrike said findings will feed into Falcon Guardian as policy recommendations.

Fiddler, the second acquisition, will bring agent observability and explainability capabilities to Falcon. CrowdStrike said the technology is intended to address risks that can arise even when agents have not been compromised.

“An agent can hold valid credentials and approved tools and still make unsupported decisions, ignore instructions, or claim work it never completed. They don’t have to be compromised to create risk,” the company said in a statement.

CrowdStrike plans to offer Fiddler’s technology through Falcon Observe. The product will evaluate agent accuracy, task completion, and policy compliance before deployment, and trace decisions, reasoning paths, and tool calls once agents are in production, the company said.

The company further added that Falcon Observe will also detect behavioural drift, hallucinations and unintended actions, while maintaining records of agent activity for compliance and audit purposes. The offering is expected to support OpenTelemetry and frameworks including LangGraph, Amazon Bedrock, AWS Strands and Google ADK, it added.

Governance remains a shared responsibility

The addition of observability and automated testing to a security platform could help enterprises correlate agent behaviour with identity, runtime activity and security events, said Apeksha Kaushik, senior principal analyst at Gartner.

However, Kaushik said the acquisitions would not make security teams the sole owners of AI agent governance. Platform and observability teams would continue to be responsible for reliability, performance and operational telemetry, while application security and AI teams would retain responsibility for secure development and testing.

“Business, data and compliance leaders also retain accountability for use cases, data and regulatory obligations,” Kaushik said.

She said CIOs should establish a governance model that defines responsibilities across engineering, security, risk, and business teams. CISOs, meanwhile, should ensure security teams have the authority to set minimum controls, monitor agent behaviour and intervene when activity creates unacceptable risk.

Integration and roadmap questions

CrowdStrike expects both transactions to close during its fourth quarter of fiscal 2027, subject to customary closing conditions, and has scheduled both offerings for general availability in the same quarter.

Kaushik cautioned enterprises against treating the announced timelines as confirmation of final product capabilities or integration plans.

“Enterprises should distinguish between announced plans and demonstrated product capability, with closing timeline and conditions possibly being different, especially with the pace of change of the threat landscape and evolution of AI,” she added.

She advised customers to seek clarity on pricing, packaging, migration terms, service continuity, support commitments, deployment models, data handling, telemetry retention and API access.

“Once the Existing and prospective customers have further details, they should set up their roadmap changes, support commitments, service continuity, contract and pricing, data portability, open integrations, and access to historical data changes,” she pointed out. CrowdStrike did not disclose the financial terms of either acquisition.

4c009f25d133.text:
An attacker has compromised the update infrastructure of cPGuard, a security suite for Linux web hosting servers, and pushed out a malicious update to nearly 3,000 customer servers.

OPSShield, the company behind the security suite, also confirmed that the attacker made off with customer contact information and hashed passwords from the firm’s billing and licensing server.

How the attack unfolded

The attacker uploaded fake cPGuard updates – versions 5.88.12 through 5.88.19 – to OPSShield’s update storage on November 2, 2026, between 02:04 and 02:09, UTC.

For the next 70+ minutes, cPGuard agents installed the fake update on about 2,950 customer servers and ran it as root.

The fake update was a short script that collected sensitive files and sent them to a server controlled by the attacker. In an earlier report on the incident, OPSShield said that the latter was OPSSHIELD’s own licensing server, where the stolen info was stored under a compromised account for the attacker to retrieve later.

The collected and exfiltrated data includes password hashes, root SSH keys, the MySQL root password (where present), root shell history (which may include typed passwords and tokens), and cloud storage keys.

“[The script] also left two pieces behind: a hidden root shell at /var/tmp/.cpg91511_sh with files in /var/tmp/.i93677/,” the company added.

According to OPSShield’s report, the day before the compromise of the update infrastructure the attacker probed OPSShield’s billing portal. They registered a customer account under a false identity, ordered a free cPGuard trial, and installed it to study how the agent talks to the licensing system.

An hour and a half later, the attacker sent crafted requests to the billing portal’s callback pages and, just minutes after that, gained the ability to run commands on the billing and licensing server, then started collecting client account records: the name, company, postal address, email, and bcrypt-hashed password of about 7,900 customers.

“Attacks like this one are getting faster and cheaper to run. Attackers now use AI tools to scan for weak points, read unfamiliar code and write custom tools in hours instead of weeks; the speed of this attack, from first probe to fake update in about ten hours, reflects that,” OPSShield noted.

The attackers also made copies of three of the company’s cloud servers.

What OPSShield has done so far

OPSShield has yet to determine how the attacker got ahold of the access/update key that allowed them to upload the fake cPGuard updates. They also don’t know yet how the attacker managed to run commands on their billing and licensing server.

“Our logs do not record the exact request that gave them access, so we are reviewing that code, patched two possible entry points that we found and verify the related vendor components line by line. We have ruled out SSH, the control panel, FTP, API tokens, etc,” the company shared.

The investigation is still ongoing. In the meantime, OPSShield has cut off the attacker’s access to every system it knows was reached.

The company revoked the stolen update-storage key along with all cloud API tokens and access keys; removed the attacker’s SSH key, cloned servers and snapshots from its cloud account; and enabled stronger login protection.

For customers, it has released a clean update (v5.88.26) which removes the hidden root shell planted by the malicious update, and a follow-up update removes the i93677 scheduled task.

OPSShield has also replaced every SSH key and password across its own servers, reset all billing portal sessions, and rotated its billing system and reseller API keys. It is re-issuing all cPGuard license key pairs so that any copies held by the attacker become useless.

Finally, it is rebuilding billing, licensing and internal management servers from clean images with tighter PHP and web firewall settings and full request logging.

What should customers do?

First, they need to check whether a malicious cPGuard version has been installed on their servers. If it has, they need to:

Update to version 5.88.26 or later, confirm that the malicious scheduled task and root shell have been removed, and review their servers for any other signs of unauthorized changes: unfamiliar users, SSH keys, services and outbound connections, etc.

Reset passwords for root and all other password-enabled local Linux accounts from a trusted recovery environment.

Rotate affected database passwords, S3 access keys, DigitalOcean tokens, and password, API key or tokens recorded in root’s shell history, as well as any keys in /root/.s3cfg.

Replace SSH private keys stored under /root/.ssh and remove the corresponding old public keys from every system that trusts them.

Reset their OPSSHIELD billing portal password (as a precaution) and turn on two-factor login.

Because cPGuard checks for updates at intervals, not every customer server received the fake update. “If cPGuard was not online during that window, your server did not receive the fake update,” OPSShield said.

For customers it has contacted directly to confirm that the attacker logged in to their server by hand, the company recommends rebuilding the server from a clean backup taken before November 1.

OPSShield published a list of indicators of compromise that also include some found on their own servers, and offered to help customers go through the remediation process.

A long-running international operation to disrupt a multimillion-dollar investment fraud operation scored another impressive victory this week after police seized 100 servers and shuttered several scam websites.

Led by the German Itzehoe Public Prosecutor's Office, the action day on November 3 targeted the company believed to be responsible for hosting the fraudulent investment websites.

Victims were lured to these sites by deceptive ads promising huge gains with no downside. After they recorded their interest, personal data would be shared by the company with criminal groups operating scam call centers, according to Europol.

Scammers impersonating brokers then used a variety of social engineering tactics to persuade the victims to invest their funds in the fictitious schemes. Online accounts set up to perpetrate the scheme apparently displayed illusory gains, persuading them to plough more money into the funds.

When victims asked to withdraw their money, brokers used delaying tactics to block payments before cutting contact and leaving them with no way to recover their funds, Europol claimed.

Investigators estimate losses to exceed €4m ($4.5m), with potential victims in as many as 50 countries.

Read more on investment fraud: Cops Arrest Suspected Multimillion-Dollar Fraud Mastermind.

Alongside the server seizures, the action day on Tuesday resulted in the arrest of seven suspects who will be extradited to Germany. Authorities also searched 17 locations and seized other evidence and assets.

The operation involved cooperation from Albania, Cyprus, Finland, Germany, Israel, Kosovo, and North Macedonia, highlighting the transnational nature of this fraud scheme. Scam call centers have been identified in Albania, Kosovo and North Macedonia, according to Europol.

Four Years in the Making

The case dates back to 2022, when a German couple complained to local authorities that they couldn’t withdraw their funds from an investment scheme they had enrolled in.

An action day on September 6, 2022, led to searches in Belgium and Latvia, and the arrest of two suspects. Evidence was seized which helped police identify seven other members of the network, including the managers of call centers which were used in the scams.

Another action day came on May 13, 2025, when police conducted eight searches simultaneously in Albania, Cyprus and Israel. That resulted in the arrest of one suspect in Cyprus and the seizure of more evidence including electronic devices, documents and cash, Europol said at the time.

Police are not claiming, as they have done in the past, to have dismantled the network.

According to the FBI, investment fraud was the highest-grossing cybercrime type in 2025, amassing nearly $8.7bn for cybercriminals. Other schemes that have come to light in Europe over recent years include an €89m ($100m) ring that was smashed in 2023 and a financial crime organization that made €15m ($17m) until it was disrupted in 2021.

6d4a91d68c01.text:
mSeven Software is warning current and former mSecure password manager customers to change passwords, reset two-factor authentication, and remove passkeys following a cyberattack in which a hacker reportedly stole an encrypted customer database..

In a security notification sent to customers on November 3 and shared with BleepingComputer, the company said it recently discovered suspicious activity involving its mSecure password management application.

"mSeven Software (“mSeven”) recently learned of suspicious activity associated with the mSecure password management application," reads the mSecure security notification.

"In response, mSeven quickly launched an investigation, took steps to mitigate the issue, and engaged external cybersecurity experts to assist. You are receiving this email because you are a current or former mSecure customer."

The notice did not provide any details as to what systems were compromised, whether customer data was stolen, and how many users were impacted.

However, the company urged all current and former customers to immediately protect confidential information stored in the password manager.

"This may include changing passwords, resetting or re-enrolling two-factor authentication methods, or removing existing passkeys," continued the security notice.

mSecure is a password manager that allows users to store passwords, passkeys, financial information, and other sensitive data in encrypted vaults that can be synchronized across devices.

According to mSeven's security documentation, mSecure uses AES-256 encryption and a zero-knowledge architecture that encrypts data locally on users' devices before transmitting it to the company's servers. The company says it cannot access customers' decrypted vault contents.

These security protections have led to confusion among customers about why they are being advised to change all their stored passwords and authentication if their data was encrypted before being uploaded to the company's servers.

Encrypted password database reportedly stolen

While the original notification had few details, customers have shared responses reportedly received from mSeven's support team indicating that a hacker stole an encrypted database from mSecure Cloud.

In one support forum post, a customer shared a response stating that the stolen database contained information belonging to current and former mSecure users.

According to the response, mSeven discovered the theft and subsequently notified customers.

The response also stated that the company had no evidence that the attacker accessed the confidential information stored within the encrypted database.

"Please note, this issue only pertains to users that were synching with the mSecure Cloud," reads the response shared by the customer.

The company also reportedly said it had implemented additional security measures and had no evidence that the mSecure application was currently unsafe to use.

Other customers reported receiving similar explanations, including confirmation that the incident was limited to users who synchronized their password databases through mSecure Cloud.

However, customers have expressed frustration over the company's lack of transparency about the breach and the potential risks to their stored credentials, particularly as mSeven has not publicly explained how the breach occurred.

While mSeven reportedly has no evidence that attackers accessed the encrypted information, stolen password vaults can still pose significant risks if attackers can crack weak master passwords through offline attacks.

This was shown in the 2022 LastPass breach, when attackers stole backups containing encrypted password vaults.

Researchers later linked the breach to cryptocurrency thefts in which attackers are believed to have cracked weak master passwords to access stored credentials, private keys, and recovery phrases.

BleepingComputer contacted mSeven Software with questions about the incident, the stolen database, and the potential impact on customers, but has not yet received a response.

0600a6582869.text:
Indian IT security company OpsShield on Monday fell victim to a cyberattack that resulted in malicious versions of cPGuard being served to its customers.

OpsShield specializes in server protection and web security software, and cPGuard is its most notable product, designed for Linux web hosting servers.

According to the company’s incident notice, the attackers used compromised credentials to access its update distribution infrastructure (CDN) and distribute a malicious script via cPGuard’s update channel.

cPGuard versions 5.88.12–5.88.19 contained the malicious code. The supply chain attack was discovered within 12 hours and the fake updates were distributed for roughly 70 minutes.

The attackers first targeted the company’s billing and licensing server. They registered a customer account and ordered a free cPGuard trial to study its communication with the licensing system, then started sending crafted requests to the portal.

After obtaining command execution on the billing and licensing server, the hackers started collecting data and then uploaded a fake cPGuard update using a stolen access key, the company explains in an updated report.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

The update was executed as root on the servers that polled OpsShield’s update infrastructure during the compromise window. At the same time, the attackers copied three of the company’s cloud servers.

The malicious script in the updates was designed to collect data and upload it to OpsShield’s licensing server under a compromised account. According to the company, the hackers retrieved 32 collected files from the data uploaded by the script, each from a different customer server.

Additionally, the script deployed a hidden root shell and certain files in the temp folder of customers’ servers.

OpsShield estimates that 2,950 servers executed the fake cPGuard updates, and that the attackers copied approximately 7,900 client account records containing names, company, addresses, emails, and hashed passwords.

All password hashes, root SSH keys, and MySQL root passwords, as well as shell history on the infected customer servers, should be considered compromised and rotated.

“If cPGuard was not online during that window, your server did not receive the fake update. You should still reset your billing portal password,” OpsShield says.

The company says it evicted the attackers from all servers they may have touched, reset secrets on its account, removed the attacker’s SSH key and cloned assets from its cloud account, and replaced all SSH keys and passwords across its servers.

Additionally, it started reissuing all cPGuard license private/public keys because the attackers compromised them, reset all billing portal login sessions and rotated associated API keys, and is rebuilding its billing, licensing, and internal management servers.

OpsShield also released cPGuard updates (version 5.88.25 and later) that remove the hidden root shell and the additional files left behind by the script, and published indicators of compromise (IoCs).

“Attacks like this one are getting faster and cheaper to run. Our answer is to harden our own update and signing process first, and then to put what we learned here straight back into cPGuard for you,” the company notes.

Related: Malicious Claude Code Extension Served in Cursor Supply Chain Attack

63c9fc3d4bdd.text:
Binance says the hackers behind last week’s $6.34 billion theft reached its wallet signing systems after a months-long campaign that compromised three engineers’ computers, one of them through a fake job interview.

The exchange published its initial incident report on November 3. Roughly $2.85 billion of the stolen assets has been frozen or intercepted.

“This should not have happened, and we apologise for the concern, disruption and uncertainty it caused our users, partners and the wider industry,” Binance said.

The FBI has blamed the theft on TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-sponsored hacking group.

How the attack unfolded

According to Binance, the intrusion unfolded in stages and relied on fake recruiters, malicious downloads, hijacked employee computers and an internal AI tool. “It was not a single isolated breach or a simple phishing incident,” the company noted.

The campaign started in June, when a Wallet DevOps engineer downloaded a tampered Homebrew installation while looking for a popular AI coding tool through a search engine.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

Binance’s security team caught it, swapped out his device and reset the related credentials. Even so, the attackers had already gained insight into what he did and who he worked with on the wallet infrastructure team.

In September, a second engineer was approached by someone claiming to be a project director. He was invited to two interviews, the first with a fake HR representative and the second with the alleged CEO of a company that did not exist.

During the first interview, the HR impostor shared a social media account containing personal photos and videos to build rapport. The second took place over a chat app and ended with a request to download a coding “assignment” onto his work computer.

The assignment hid a malicious code repository that executed as soon as the engineer set it up. The malware substituted a rogue copy of a legitimate developer tool component and opened a channel to a server run by the attackers.

“The 0-day malware was not detected by the endpoint security protection tools at the time,” Binance said.

On October 20, the attackers used the infected machine and an internal AI tool to gain control of the first engineer’s system and a third wallet engineer’s system. The report does not explain how the AI tool was used.

The first engineer’s computer held a token that allowed container deployments. On October 29, the attackers signed into the third engineer’s computer, deployed a container with credentials taken from the first engineer and kicked off the attack with a malicious script.

Binance says the attackers exploited unauthorized access to an internal wallet signing service to move XRP, SOL, OP and BTC out of its hot wallets. The same service was used to abuse Ethereum’s EIP-7702 mechanism, giving a contract under the attackers’ control partial execution rights over a hot wallet.

“However, suspending withdrawals alone could not stop all unauthorized asset movements. The malicious EIP-7702 authorizations existed on-chain and operated independently of Binance’s normal withdrawal infrastructure,” the company explained.

The hot wallet was secured with multi-party computation (MPC), which meant Binance had no single key it could use to cancel the delegation right away. The last unauthorized transfer settled at 23:56 UTC, and the delegation was cleared shortly after midnight.

Binance says it has rebuilt the affected wallet system and AI tool, replaced devices and retired the engineers’ credentials and tokens. It is engaging independent security firms to review the incident and is working on a research fund focused on AI security in blockchain environments.

The exchange also disclosed that it had detected and blocked 57 suspected North Korea-linked threats this year.

Other developments

North Korea has rejected the FBI’s attribution of the heist to its TraderTraitor hackers. “It is a grave political provocation against the DPRK that the US misleads international public opinion as if all the cyber crimes in different parts of the world are our deeds,” Kim Yo Jong, sister of leader Kim Jong Un, said in a statement carried by state media.

[ Read: North Korea Launches Missiles Toward the Sea to Protest Binance Hack Claims ]

Binance has also completed a zero-knowledge proof for its October 31 reserves snapshot, which lets holders of 10 major tokens verify that their balances are backed at least 1:1. Co-CEO Richard Teng says 98% of the impacted tokens have now been replenished.

Teng also said on November 3 that withdrawals have broadly resumed. The exchange began reopening them in phases on November 1.

On the laundering front, Elliptic says the stolen funds passed through about 12,000 wallets on 11 blockchains in under four days, using automation but with no sign of AI agents making decisions. As of November 3, roughly $3.18 billion remained in theft-linked addresses. Separately, Chainalysis said an emergency pause at THORChain, triggered by an unrelated technical issue, had temporarily slowed the laundering.

Related: Chainalysis Discloses Data Breach Following AI-Driven Cyberattack

Related: Polymarket Returns $3.9 Million to Traders as DebugBear Cites DNS Hijack

75201b272e41.text:
Critical Android flaw CVE-2026-58868 could allow remote code execution without user interaction on devices running Android 14 through 17.

Google has fixed CVE-2026-58868, a critical Android vulnerability affecting versions 14 through 17. The flaw is a critical Android vulnerability caused by a heap buffer overflow in the onOutputReceived function of FrameDecoder.cpp. The flaw can trigger an out-of-bounds write, potentially allowing a remote attacker to execute arbitrary code on a vulnerable device. Exploitation requires neither user interaction nor additional execution privileges, making it a potential zero-click attack.

“cve-2026-58868 In onOutputReceived of FrameDecoder.cpp, there is a possible out-of-bounds write due to a heap buffer overflow.” reads the advisory. “This could lead to remote code execution with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation.”

Devices receive the fix through security patch level 2026-11-01 or later, depending on manufacturers and carriers. Google is now aware of active exploitation of the flaws in its November 2026 bulletin.

Google’s November 2026 Android security bulletin addresses 216 vulnerabilities, including 23 rated Critical. Two of these flaws, CVE-2026-58876 and CVE-2026-58936, affect the System component and could allow remote code execution without user interaction.

The bulletin also lists five other Critical flaws in the System component. Three could lead to privilege escalation, while two could cause denial-of-service conditions. Another Critical vulnerability affects the Framework component and could also allow remote code execution.

Six Critical vulnerabilities affect the Android kernel. Two involve Bluetooth code, three affect the protected Kernel-based Virtual Machine (pKVM), and one is in the Human Interface Device (HID) component. The most severe kernel flaw could allow a remote attacker to gain elevated privileges without user interaction.

The November 5 patch level also addresses Critical vulnerabilities in MediaTek modem code and a closed-source Qualcomm component. Google’s bulletin lists eight Critical MediaTek modem flaws, while MediaTek’s own November security bulletin details six of them: CVE-2026-20499 and CVE-2026-20545 through CVE-2026-20549.

MediaTek describes these six vulnerabilities as out-of-bounds write flaws caused by missing bounds checks, integer overflow or improper input validation. The company says it is not aware of any active exploitation in the wild.

The Qualcomm issue is tracked as CVE-2026-25285 and affects a closed-source component. Google does not provide further technical details in its bulletin.

One of the critical issues fixed by Google is CVE-2026-58882 (aka SMS of Death), which could allow attackers to remotely disable a phone by sending a specially crafted SMS message. The flaw affects decodeWapPdu, a function responsible for processing WAP Push messages, a type of content delivered through the SMS infrastructure.

The vulnerability is particularly concerning because exploitation reportedly requires no user interaction. An attacker only needs the victim’s phone number to send a malicious message. The message doesn’t appear in the SMS inbox, so the victim may have no indication of what caused the problem.

The issue also raises concerns about the reliability of mobile communications during an attack. According to a technical analysis published on October 29 by security researcher Mark B, a malformed WAP Push message can crash com.android.phone, the Android system component responsible for handling telephony functions. The crash can terminate ongoing calls, including emergency calls.

Tests on several Android phone models reportedly reproduced the crash consistently. The phone can also become stuck in a crash loop because Android retries processing the malicious message whenever the device starts. As a result, the device may continue crashing until the offending message is removed.

There is an important distinction, however. Google’s security bulletin and the CVE record identify the vulnerable decodeWapPdu function, but neither explicitly confirms that CVE-2026-58882 is the same issue described in the researcher’s SMS of Death report. The technical overlap is worth investigating, but the two reports shouldn’t be treated as definitively describing the same vulnerability without further confirmation.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, CVE-2026-58868)

f426076d05cb.text:
Since mid-August 2026, a phishing operation has been harvesting live Google sessions from corporate users. Every signal defenders usually rely on to judge a link returned a reassuring answer, and the operator built the chain that way on purpose.

Material Security’s Threat Research team identified the campaign and has taken down hundreds of domains used by attackers in what they have dubbed Operation CloudFire. Here’s what they learned along the way.

The lure: Google Calendar invites

The messages arrive as Google Calendar invites, sometimes delivered by BCC and often sent from an organization the recipient has already corresponded with. The pretexts are mundane: voicemail notifications, RFP and RFI requests, court summonses, and missed payment notices.

Most links point to Google itself. The typical pattern is Google’s own /url redirector with the real destination in a query parameter, though other waves used share.google and Drive file links for the same purpose. One variant used Intuit transaction notification links.

In every case, when the message is scored, the domain, certificate, and reputation displayed are legitimate and trusted.

The capture: Reverse proxy in front of a Google sign-in page

The attacker runs a live reverse proxy in front of the genuine Google sign-in page. The victim enters a password, receives a real prompt, and approves it, all while the operator watches the session in real time.

The server relays SMS codes, authenticator codes, Google’s Tap-Yes number matching, and phone-based account recovery to Google as each one arrives, so none of the second-factor controls stop the session from being captured.

The framework behind this, Nyasher, has been documented publicly since February, after a hardcoded key was found in its JavaScript.

Why the controls don’t fire

Reputation systems answer a question about ownership: who registered the domain, what else it has hosted, and whether anyone has complained about it. This campaign was assembled so that those answers were consistently benign, and it has three layers.

The first layer is Google’s redirector. The second is a Cloudflare Turnstile challenge, which in some builds is the genuine widget served from Cloudflare’s own infrastructure. The third layer is the password-capture page itself, which has no static website to scan.

The Javascript constructs it in the browser after the visitor clears the challenge, so a crawler has nothing to fetch and a proxy log has nothing to record. To Material’s knowledge, no one had scanned those pages before the campaign was documented.

The infrastructure is disposable by design. The initially observed campaign used many lure domains across multiple registrars, most registered only days before use. Receiving endpoints were staged one to twenty days ahead of the wave they served.

One wildcard certificate was issued 46 minutes before the domain it covers was registered. Blocking any single component costs the operator a few dollars and an afternoon of work.

Automated Email Security for Google Workspace & Microsoft 365

Material detects and remediates phishing, BEC, and targeted attacks automatically, even after delivery.

No complex rulesets, no user quarantines, no endless manual triage.

Get a Demo

What defending it has looked like

Material has tracked the campaign since its start, following each variant as lures, gates, and receiving endpoints rotated. Since August, once the campaign was identified and detections built, Material has caught over 99% of the malicious messages, with a reclassification rate of 0.01%.

This has been a continuous effort as the attacker shifted their TTP’s, themes and lure text to evade static, ML and agentic detections.

The approach works because no single signal decides the outcome. Reputation alone would not have caught this, and neither would link analysis by itself, since the first hop is a Google URL and the final page doesn’t exist until a browser constructs it.

Material scores technical indicators, the apparent intent of the message, where links actually resolve, and the sending relationship behind the message. Any one of those can be enough to act on.

A detection built around one signal inherits that signal’s blind spots, and this operator has spent considerable effort mapping them.

Where the analysis runs also matters. A calendar invite is a poor fit for a gateway designed to inspect mail in transit, yet much of this campaign arrives as an invite.

Material treats calendar invites as a threat surface in their own right and uses the account’s full history as context alongside the technical signals.

Where the damage lands

When the outcome is a hijacked session rather than a stolen password, the evidence appears in Workspace audit logs. A live Google session reaches mail, Drive, and the ability to grant OAuth access in the victim’s name, so the blast radius extends well past the inbox.

Defenders should ask two questions: who is reviewing those logs, and how quickly can they be acted on? Equally important is whether the team can revoke sessions, contain OAuth grants, and reset the affected account within an hour.

Many programs cannot, and an attacker with a live session can do a great deal in that time.

Operation CloudFire: Targeting the infrastructure

By late September, Material concluded that tuning rules, retraining models, and updating agents would not solve the problem alone. Detection protects customers but does nothing about the operator who is preparing the next wave.

Material’s Threat Research team therefore launched Operation CloudFire to target the infrastructure itself.

The team analyzed the gateway and backend URLs as the messages were being sent and reported them through Cloudflare’s abuse reporting system. Cloudflare’s abuse team validated the fake interstitial and the proxied Google sign-in page behind it, then applied its own phishing interstitial to those destinations.

This had two effects. The attacker’s infrastructure was burned: each reported gateway and receiving endpoint had to be re-registered, re-pointed, and re-certified before the operator could send again. The broader internet also benefited.

Anyone who clicked a reported link, whether or not they were a Material customer, saw a warning rather than a credential form.

The numbers over one month

These figures come only from customers who agreed to share data with Material, so the true totals are higher. Over a month of Operation CloudFire, Material recorded:

68,676 campaign messages blocked

2,112 unique malicious URLs analyzed

897 unique domains taken down

8,570 unique compromised sender addresses across 6,354 root domains

Send cadence that followed US business hours

The sender count shows how the campaign achieved its credibility. Each compromised address belonged to an account the attacker controlled before the first invite went out, and each one sent invites to the victim’s saved contacts, among other addresses.

Recipients saw a name or domain they knew, on a domain with a clean history, at a plausible time. Reputation feeds had no reason to flag any of it, so every layer that scores ownership and history returned a reassuring result.

Where things stand

The phishing themes have shifted, from calendar invites to Google Drive file and document share invites. Material has not seen a matching rise in other lures or TTPs, and activity from this group appears to have dispersed. The campaign looks finished.

That is a status update, not a verdict. Rebuilding the infrastructure is cheap, the framework has been public since February, and the operator shipped an unfinished Microsoft 365 branch alongside the live Google code.

The branch includes a stylesheet path, a second harness, and a title string that decodes to a Microsoft sign-in prompt. None of those paths resolve today, and adding the brand requires dropping in a file rather than changing any code.

The operator has built the follow-on and has not activated it. Material reads the theme rotation as iteration, not retirement, and expects the next pivot to look much like this one with a different brand.

The full technical breakdown, including indicators and a timeline, is available in the companion whitepaper. Teams hunting for this activity in their own environments should start there.

Sponsored and written by Material Security.

SonicWall warned customers of two security flaws affecting end-of-life Global Management System (GMS) systems that will not be patched.

Global Management System (GMS) helps IT admins deploy and manage thousands of SonicWall security appliances from a single interface, but SonicWall has officially replaced it with the Network Security Manager (NSM) management platform.

The two vulnerabilities were found and reported by Pentest-Tools security researchers and affect systems running SonicWall GMS 9.5.2 and earlier.

The first GMS flaw disclosed this week is tracked as CVE-2026-109593, and it enables unauthenticated attackers with network access to vulnerable instances (running GMS 9.5.2 and earlier versions) to steal sensitive information by reading internal files.

SonicWall also flagged a second security issue (CVE-2026-109594) that can let threat actors with high privileges access or modify information stored in the GMS database through low-complexity SQL Injection attacks.

On Tuesday, SonicWall also urged customers to upgrade to NMS, as it will not release security patches because the vulnerable systems have now reached end of life.

"The affected product has reached End-of-Life (EOL). As a result, no remediation or security update will be released for these vulnerabilities," SonicWall warned on Tuesday.

"Organizations using the product should be aware of the associated security risks and are strongly encouraged to upgrade to the SonicWall Network Security Manager (NSM)."

Attackers often target SonicWall vulnerabilities in the wild and have exploited multiple ones in zero-day attacks since the start of the year.

In February, SonicWall asked customers to patch two SMA1000 zero-days (CVE-2026-15409 and CVE-2026-15410) and two more (CVE-2026-15409 and CVE-2026-15410) in July. It also patched three other SMA1000 flaws exploited as zero-days in September (CVE-2026-83548 and CVE-2026-83549) and October (CVE-2026-102255).

Over the last four years, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added 19 SonicWall vulnerabilities to its list of actively exploited flaws, 13 of them also abused by ransomware gangs.

SonicWall serves more than 500,000 customers (including small and medium-sized businesses, large enterprises, and government agencies) in more than 215 countries and territories through a network of over 17,000 partners.

d65450d3891e.text:
Threat actors targeted multiple software engineers at Binance with sophisticated social engineering and zero-day malware in a months-long campaign that led to a record-breaking digital heist last week, the crypto exchange has revealed.

Binance revealed the news in a lengthy post on X (formerly Twitter) on November 3.

“It was not a single isolated breach or a simple phishing incident,” it explained.

“The attackers combined a range of techniques, including social engineering by fake recruitment interviews, malicious software downloads, compromised internal AI tooling, endpoint compromise, and an advanced transaction-authorisation method.”

Read more on crypto theft: Hackers Exploit BTCPay Server Flaw to Steal Cryptocurrency.

The main point of intrusion appears to have stemmed from an interview the threat group set up with an unnamed “Software Engineer B” in September.

An individual posing as a project director contacted the engineer via a legitimate job-hunting platform, having spotted from their profile that they worked at Binance.

The first-round interview was held with a fictitious HR representative, during which the interviewer shared a social media account with the engineer, including personal photos and videos posted, in order to build trust, Binance said.

“The second interview was conducted in a popular social chat app, near the end of the interview, Engineer B was instructed to download an ‘assignment’ containing a malicious code repository onto his work computer,” it continued. “The repository contained malicious code that executed during the setup process, initiating a series of unauthorized activities.”

According to Binance, the “zero-day malware” used obfuscation and evasion techniques to ensure it was not detected by the engineer’s endpoint security tools. These included replacing a legitimate development tool component with a malicious version to execute commands and connect with a C2 server.

The Pathway to Wallet-Signing Operations

On October 20, the attacker accessed an internal AI tool via Engineer B’s computer to compromise the machines of two other Binance employees: Wallet DevOps Engineer A and Wallet Software Engineer C.

The former had been scoped out back in June when they unwittingly downloaded a malicious version of Homebrew, a third-party package manager for macOS, after clicking on a malicious search ad.

Although the Binance team “detected the anomaly, replaced the device, and rotated all related credentials” at the time, the engineer’s role and those of his colleagues had already been exposed to the hackers.

After compromising Engineer A’s machine, they found out he had a container deployment permission token on his computer.

“On October 29 between 17:15 and 19:56, the attacker logged onto Software Engineer C’s computer, used the credentials stolen from Wallet DevOps Engineer A, deployed a container, and triggered a malicious script to launch the attack,” the report explained.

Between 20:05 UTC and 20:09 UTC, five Binance hot wallets then sent 233.46 million XRP to an attacker-controlled address, while Binance hot wallets on Solana and Optimism sent around 970,500 SOL and 44.2 million OP to attacker-controlled addresses.

Clean-Up Time

Binance said it has since rebuilt the affected wallet system and internal AI tool along with the latter’s access controls, and that it has replaced affected devices.

It also decommissioned engineer credentials and tokens, enhanced security scans across employee devices, improved AI-based behavioral anomaly detection and strengthened wallet service risk controls.

The firm admitted it had already detected and prevented 57 suspected North Korean attacks this year alone. It is currently conducting a review of the incident, setting up a security research fund with industry partners, and has already increased investment in AI-enabled detection, protection and monitoring tools.

Experts from Fortra questioned the controls that were originally in place to protect employee, and especially developer, machines.

“In a world where quiet quitting exists, it should come as no surprise that employees are interviewing on company time. Organizations need to counter this with adequate controls in place. Particularly, controls around what can be downloaded and executed on a corporate laptop, as well as the permissions granted to the user,” argued Tyler Reguly, associate director, security R&D at Fortra.

“At the end of the day, developer laptops are among the hardest devices in an organization to lock down safely without being detrimental. Organizations need to find the balance point."

North Korea launched multiple missiles toward the sea on Wednesday, South Korea’s military said, hours after Pyongyang said it saw no need to resume diplomacy with Washington in protest of accusations that North Korean hackers were behind the recent cryptocurrency heist at Binance.

Observers say North Korea was likely pressuring the U.S. to drop what it calls its hostility against the North and offer concessions if it wants to restore ties between U.S. President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said it detected the launches of several missiles fired toward North Korea’s eastern waters. It said South Korean and U.S. authorities were analyzing details of the launches. It said South Korea maintains readiness to repel any potential provocations by North Korea.

Earlier Wednesday, Kim’s sister, senior official Kim Yo Jong, again disputed an FBI announcement that North Korean hackers were responsible for the hack at Binance, calling it “an extension of Washington’s invariable hostile policy toward” Pyongyang.

“It is our clear stand that we have no need to sit face to face with such unreliable and hostile persons,” she said. “The choice for peace includes dialogue of course, but this is not surely equated with national interests for us.”

In a Tuesday statement, she described the FBI announcement as “a trite provocation.”

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

Binance, the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange, said Friday that hackers stole more than $6 billion in what appears to be the largest cryptocurrency heist on record. The FBI later said the theft was orchestrated by North Korean hackers, attributing the attack to a hacking group known as TraderTraitor, which was also behind a $1.5 billion hack of the Bybit exchange last year.

In recent months, North Korea has accelerated its weapons tests in a likely bid to increase its leverage in potential diplomacy with the U.S. after Trump expressed his eagerness to restore diplomacy with Kim Jong Un. The news of the latest launches came amid vote counting in the U.S. midterm elections.

Also Wednesday, North Korea’s state KCNA news agency released a photo showing parts of a warship under construction that would likely be its biggest naval vessel. KCNA said Kim Jong Un expressed satisfaction this week during a visit to the Nampho Shipyard over the warship that it said “is incomparably huge” relative to its 5,000-ton destroyers. Kim previously said North Korea planned to build a 10,000-ton strategic guided missile cruiser.

Tensions between the two Koreas have also deepened since mine blasts at their border in September wounded three South Korean soldiers. Seoul accused North Korea of burying the mines south of the border and demanded an apology. Pyongyang has denied responsibility for the explosions and warned of retaliation if provoked.

North Korea later threatened to resume propaganda loudspeaker broadcasts and place new weapons systems along the border.

707c59bed9d4.text:
Executive Summary

PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) allows unauthenticated remote code execution on exposed PHP servers. PHP has released fixed versions. On Linux, distribution packages carry the fix. On Windows and macOS, they don’t: Microsoft and Apple don’t ship PHP, so the fix is an in-place PHP upgrade that has traditionally been done by hand, one server at a time. Qualys TruRisk Eliminate’s Custom Assessment and Remediation (CAR) capability runs Qualys TRU-published scripts that upgrade each PHP installation to the latest patch release of its current minor series. On Windows, the script verifies the official build by SHA256 and rolls back on failure. On macOS, it upgrades through Homebrew. If a host is on an end-of-life series, the script stops, reports it, and then you apply the PHP2Shell mitigation script instead. The same script runs through the Cloud Agent or, on hosts without one, through an authenticated Qualys scanner. Agentless runs need a Windows or SSH credential with rights to stop services and replace PHP binaries. Plan a maintenance window for both because IIS, Apache, or php-fpm restarts during the upgrade.

PHP has released a critical security update addressing two vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (collectively tracked as PHP2Shell), that allow unauthenticated remote code execution against exposed PHP servers.

On Linux, patching is straightforward: distribution vendors ship updated packages, and Qualys TruRisk Eliminate deploys them.

Windows and macOS are a different story. There is no straightforward vendor patch to deploy, so the fix must be a PHP upgrade, which has traditionally required someone to log in to each server and apply it manually. This blog explains how the Qualys Custom Assessment and Remediation (CAR) capability in Qualys TruRisk Eliminate closes the gap for both deployment models: agent-based and agentless (scanner-based).

Why Patch Management Can’t Deliver the Fix on Windows and macOS

Patching works by deploying the fix that an operating system or software vendor publishes. For PHP on Windows and macOS, that fix does not exist in a deployable form.

Windows: no official installer or updater. Microsoft does not ship PHP, and PHP does not ship an installer or an in-place updater for Windows. The official builds on downloads.php.net are plain ZIP archives published in multiple flavors (Thread Safe / Non-Thread Safe, x64 / x86, and per Visual Studio compiler). Upgrading means picking the right build, stopping IIS or Apache, replacing the binaries in place while preserving php.ini and custom extensions, and restarting services. Third-party stacks such as XAMPP, WampServer, Laragon, Chocolatey and Scoop each add their own layout on top of that.

macOS: Apple no longer ships PHP. PHP was removed from macOS in Monterey (12.0), and Apple software updates do not touch it. php.net publishes only source code, so on modern Macs, PHP most commonly comes from Homebrew (the php formula or a versioned php@8.x formula).

The result is that a PHP server on Windows or macOS will appear vulnerable, with no corresponding patch in the TruRisk Eliminate patch catalog. The vulnerability is real; the remediation path is not a patch.

Custom Assessment and Remediation Closes the Gap with TruRisk Eliminate

TruRisk Eliminate covers four remediation paths: patch, mitigate, isolate, or run a custom script. PHP on Windows and macOS needs the fourth. The CAR capability in TruRisk Eliminate lets you run controlled remediation scripts on your assets from the same platform that detected the exposure. The Qualys Threat Research Unit (TRU) has published PHP upgrade scripts for Windows and macOS in the CAR library so that every host is upgraded the same way. Search the library for “PHP Update to Latest Patch Version” under the PHP2Shell category and import the script for each platform.

Figure 1: PHP2Shell category in the CAR script library. Figure 2: The PHP Update to Latest Patch Version script in the CAR script library (PHP2Shell category).

Both scripts are built around the same principles:

Upgrade within the installed minor series only. 8.2.33 moves to the latest 8.2.x, 8.4.27 to the latest 8.4.x. The scripts never jump a major or minor version, so applications keep running on the branch they were tested against.

Mitigate what can’t be upgraded. If the installed series is end-of-life and no longer published, the script stops and reports it instead of guessing. For those hosts, deploy the PHP2Shell mitigation script from the CAR library. It applies configuration changes that block the attack path and restarts the affected services. Mitigation reduces the risk until you can move to a supported branch; it doesn’t replace the upgrade.

Windows: Official Builds, Verified and Rolled Back on Failure

Discovers every PHP installation on the host, not just the one on PATH: machine and per-user PATH entries, common folders (C:\php*, XAMPP, WAMP, Laragon, Program Files, Scoop), IIS FastCGI handlers in applicationHost.config, and any Windows service that launches a PHP binary.

Detects each installation’s exact build flavor (TS/NTS, x64/x86, VC15/VS16/VS17) by querying php.exe itself, then selects the matching official build from downloads.php.net/releases.json.

Honours the machine WinHTTP proxy automatically, since the SYSTEM account has no user proxy settings.

Downloads the archive and verifies its SHA256 against the published hash before anything is touched.

Stops IIS (W3SVC/WAS), Apache and any php/php-cgi processes using that directory, takes a full backup of the PHP folder, copies the new binaries over the top (php.ini and extra extensions are preserved), and confirms the new version by running php.exe.

Rolls back from the backup and restarts services automatically if the post-upgrade version check fails.

macOS: Homebrew Upgrades Within the Same PHP Series

The macOS script handles the realities of Homebrew, as follows:

Confirms PHP is present and resolves the real binary through symlinks into the Homebrew Cellar to determine which formula owns it (php or php@8.x). PHP from MacPorts, MAMP or a manual build is reported and left alone.

Runs brew as the user who owns the Homebrew installation, because Homebrew refuses to run as root even though CAR executes as root. It also repairs any Homebrew files left owned by root from earlier runs so brew can write to them.

Refreshes Homebrew with retry handling for the common “another brew update is already running” case, and falls back to cached formula data if the refresh fails.

Stays on the installed series. If the default PHP formula has moved to a newer series (for example, the host is on 8.2.x but PHP now tracks 8.4), the script installs or upgrades PHP 8.2 and relinks the PHP command to it rather than forcing a major upgrade.

Restarts the php-fpm service via brew services if it was running before the upgrade and prints the final php -v so the result is visible in the job output.

Agent or Agentless: The Same Script Reaches Every Host

When you create a script in CAR, you choose how it reaches the host. Agent Devices run the script locally through the installed Cloud Agent. Perimeter Devices require no Cloud Agent. The script is delivered and executed through an authenticated Qualys scanner. The script content is identical in both cases; only the delivery changes. Select Windows or Mac as the platform to match the script.

Figure 3: Creating the script in CAR. Choose Agent Devices or Perimeter Devices (agentless), then select Windows or Mac as the platform.

Agent-Based Remediation

In ETM, identify Windows and macOS hosts flagged for the PHP2Shell CVEs (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) and tag them by platform.

In CAR, create or import the Windows and macOS PHP upgrade scripts with Agent Devices selected and run each against its platform tag.

Schedule the install run in a maintenance window, since IIS, Apache, or php-fpm will be restarted.

Review job results and rescan to confirm the QID closes.

Agentless Remediation

Many exposed PHP servers sit on appliances, DMZ servers, legacy hosts, and systems owned by other teams: a Windows Server in the DMZ running a vendor web application on IIS and PHP, or Mac minis in a build lab owned by engineering. Many can’t run, or aren’t allowed to run, a Cloud Agent.

A network scan can show that these systems are exposed, but remediating them has usually required someone to log in and make changes by hand, one server at a time. With unauthenticated remote code execution on the table, that pace leaves your perimeter open.

With the CAR capability in TruRisk Eliminate, the same Windows and macOS PHP upgrade scripts run directly on scanner-based hosts through the Perimeter Devices option.

Find your scanner-only hosts. In ETM, identify exposed PHP servers using the PHP2Shell CVEs (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619).

Create the scripts for Perimeter Devices. In the CAR module of TruRisk Eliminate, select the PHP upgrade script for the host’s platform from the library, choose Perimeter Devices and Windows or Mac, and point it at the scanner appliance that can reach those hosts with the appropriate authentication records (Windows or SSH).

Run the job. Launch the job against your scanner-based hosts. The scripts behave identically whether launched from an agent or a scanner.

Confirm the remediation. Review the job output for the recorded before/after version on each host, then rerun the scan and confirm the QID no longer reports.

What the Job Output Looks Like

Each host returns a short, readable log entry with the execution status and the before/after PHP versions. Below, a scanner-based macOS host is upgraded from PHP 8.2.33 to 8.2.35 within the 8.2 series, with the php@8.2 formula relinked as the active PHP.

Figure 4: CAR job results showing the PHP upgrade output on a scanner-based macOS host.

On Windows, the log additionally lists every PHP installation discovered on the host, the detected build flavor, SHA256 verification, the services stopped and restarted, and the backup folder location.

Figure 5: CAR job results showing the PHP upgrade output on a scanner-based Windows host.

Conclusion

PHP2Shell is a reminder that remediation goes beyond patching. When there is no straightforward vendor patch to deploy, you still need a safe, fast way to close the exposure. With TruRisk Eliminate, you can discover every PHP installation, upgrade it to the latest release of its current series with integrity verification, automatic rollback, and service restart, and do it from the same console that detected the exposure, agentless on scanner-only hosts and through the Cloud Agent where it is installed.

Qualys customers can find the Windows and macOS PHP upgrade scripts, along with the PHP2Shell mitigation script, in the CAR script library. Review the CVEs (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) in ETM and begin with your internet-facing perimeter.

Not a Qualys customer? Access Qualys’ free PHP2Shell mitigation service to help protect your environment against this threat.

Sign Up for Free Mitigation Service

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

Will the script jump me from PHP 8.2 to 8.4?

No. It upgrades only within the installed minor series. 8.2.33 moves to the latest 8.2.x. Applications stay on the branch they were tested against.

What happens on an end-of-life series?

The script stops and reports it. Deploy the PHP2Shell mitigation script until you can move to a supported branch.

Does this work without a Cloud Agent?

Yes. Choose Perimeter Devices and run the same script through an authenticated Qualys scanner. You need a Windows or SSH credential with rights to stop services and replace PHP binaries.

What does the Windows script verify?

It detects the build flavor, downloads the matching official build from downloads.php.net, verifies SHA256 before anything is touched, and rolls back from a full backup if the post-upgrade version check fails.
