On 29 October 2026, attackers moved approximately $6.34 billion out of Binance's internet-connected trading wallets (hot wallets) in under four hours. The FBI attributes the theft to TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking unit. As of Binance's 3 November disclosure, roughly $2.85 billion has been frozen.

The wallet-draining mechanism is crypto-specific and most enterprise defenders will never encounter it. But the months of preparation that made it possible look like a standard enterprise breach: social engineering, a compromised developer workstation, stolen credentials, and lateral movement (moving from one system to the next) across team boundaries where no single security team saw the full chain.

A fake job interview placed the first foothold

The campaign started no later than June 2026 with a tampered software download on a Wallet DevOps engineer's machine. Binance detected it, replaced the device, and rotated credentials. The response was correct. It was also incomplete: the attacker had already mapped the wallet infrastructure team.

In September, a separate software engineer was contacted through a legitimate job platform. What followed was a two-round interview, including a live video call where the interviewer shared personal photos to build trust. Near the end of the second round, the engineer was told to download a coding "assignment." The repository replaced a legitimate development tool with a malicious binary. Binance confirms it "was not detected by the endpoint security protection tools at the time".

Nothing looked wrong:

A developer downloaded a coding assignment from a job interview.

The binary sat where the legitimate tool had been.

The security software on the engineer's machine had nothing to match it against.

The AI tool was the corridor between teams

This is the detail that turns a crypto theft into an enterprise story.

On 20 October, nine days before the theft, the attacker used the compromised engineer's machine and an internal AI tool to reach two other engineers on the wallet team. Binance's disclosure confirms the attacker "leveraged the compromised computer of engineer B and used an internal AI tool to gain control over" Engineers A and C. The tool is not named.

The AI tool was a shared service that connected people across roles. The attacker was already authenticated as the compromised engineer, so interacting with the tool looked like normal use. There was no exploit of the tool itself. It was functioning exactly as designed: connecting people, sharing context, enabling collaboration. That is what made it a path for moving between teams.

Through that path, the attacker found a permission token for deploying containers on one engineer's machine. On 29 October, the attacker used it to deploy a malicious container that reached Binance's internal wallet signing service. From there, the attacker initiated unauthorized transactions using valid credentials through the normal signing path.

Three gaps in one chain

The Binance breach is unusual because all three detection gaps appear in the same incident:

‍Gap 1, nothing looks wrong: The malicious binary replaced a legitimate tool, the zero-day evaded the security software and the attacker removed traces of the compromise.

‍Gap 2, authentication succeeds: The signing service processed the attacker's requests because they arrived through the normal path with valid credentials.

‍Gap 3, movement isn't visible: The attacker crossed from a software engineer's workstation, to an internal AI tool, to Wallet DevOps credentials, to a different engineer's machine, to a container platform, to the signing service. Five hops across four functional boundaries. Each appeared in a different log.

Internal AI tools are trust boundaries nobody is watching

Most organizations adopting internal AI tools are focused on data leakage and on attackers manipulating the tool's inputs. Those are real risks. But the Binance breach shows a third: the tool itself becomes a bridge between teams, and a compromised identity on one side can walk to the other without triggering a boundary alert, because no boundary exists.

The signing service worked. The security software worked until it met a zero-day, which is what zero-days do. The credential rotation in June was the right call. Each control did its job in isolation. The gap was the chain between them, and the AI tool sitting in the middle of that chain, treated as an application rather than a trust boundary.

Detection is not broken. It is incomplete.

Network and identity telemetry close the gaps between controls

Each control in the Binance chain worked in its own lane. The problem was the space between lanes. Closing that space requires two things the individual controls do not provide: visibility into how identities behave across systems (not just whether they authenticated), and visibility into how traffic moves between hosts (not just whether it was allowed).

Network telemetry shows an internal AI tool suddenly generating access patterns it has never generated before. Identity telemetry shows a software engineer's account interacting with wallet infrastructure it has never touched. Neither signal alone is conclusive. Correlated, they are a single story: a compromised identity is walking from one team's environment into another's.

That correlation is what Vectra AI's Attack Signal Intelligence does. It connects identity behavior and network behavior across on-premises and cloud environments, including both human and non-human identities (service accounts, tokens, application credentials), and surfaces them as one attack narrative rather than isolated alerts. In a chain like Binance's, the goal is to surface the five-hop path as one event before the attacker reaches the signing service, not to flag each hop independently after the fact.

For a detailed walk-through of how these three detection gaps interact, including coverage mapping for identity, network, and cloud telemetry, see chapters 3 through 5 of the Mind Your Gaps in the Age of AI-Powered Attacks whitepaper.

aba35cbbdf00.text:
A First Look: Under the Hood of AI Agents

With early access to Sysdig AI Defense, one software development company spent a month looking at AI agent usage across their enterprise. Below is what they found.

Citizen developers are generating code

At this organization, 50% of the employees using AI agents work outside of the engineering department. Marketing, human resources, sales, legal, and finance all used AI agents daily, and they aren’t just chatting with them. Among the non-engineers using agents, an average of 42% of them had an agent run code, a build, a package install, or a cloud or cluster command.

A finance employee building tools likely doesn’t possess the same security knowledge as an engineer, nor are they likely to have the same reviews in place by default. But that shouldn’t stop them from creating. Organizations should watch installs and CLI calls and provide an approved, sandboxed path for them to build.

Tool calls are running without human approval

People turn off prompts to keep their work moving, and although it isn’t generally a sign of carelessness, it can open organizations up to greater risk. More than 60% of this organization’s tool calls ran without a human approving them — 52% screened by Claude Code’s auto-mode classifier instead of a person, and 9% with permission prompts intentionally turned off (YOLO mode).

But the answer to minimizing this risk isn’t blocking everything or turning a blind eye. Organizations need to understand their risk profiles at different levels, and allow tools, agents, and extensions based on what they can reach and change.

The agent’s account of its own actions isn’t enough

For every tool call this organization’s agents logged, the kernel captured seven processes. While an agent’s log may help a user debug a session, it’s not meant to be used as audit evidence because the agent writes it. The kernel sees what actually ran at the process level, regardless of the tool or API used. However, additional data shows that the security team needs both to see the full picture. For example, when an agent read a credential file, the agent’s log had no entry 82% of the time. However, the kernel logged every read.

Connecting unverified extensions to agents

Nearly half (47%) of the MCP servers in use came from third-party registries or vendors for this organization. Each server is a trusted relationship that only takes one line of config to connect to an agent, and once connected, it has access. Servers can also update silently in the background, so the one you trusted last week may not be the one running today.

Matching models to tasks

More than 50% of the organization’s AI spend went to duplicative processes and capabilities. With visibility into which models are used, scoped to the team and user behind each agent, organizations can tie model choice to the task and cut duplication.

What else is in the full report

This is only a fraction of what one month of agent activity uncovered. Dig deeper to discover:

How often security-relevant detections are triggered.

A risk-tier framework for allowing agents and extensions by what they can reach

Real alerts from the deployment, including a possible data exfiltration, an unapproved model provider, and a change to cloud permissions.

What model tiers employees are actually using day to day.

A risk reduction table you can hand to your team.

Odds are, AI agents are already running in your organization. The question is whether you know where they’re running, and whether you can see what they’re doing. Read the full report to see what this organization found and how you can start closing the gap.

4450970d8772.text:
AI has moved from assisting to acting. Agents now read files, run commands and reach your cloud with a real person’s access. Most of the time, the only record of what they did is the one the agent wrote itself. “A First Look: Under the Hood of AI Agents” shows where one software company's agents logged one tool call for every seven processes the kernel actually watched them run. And it isn’t only engineers. Someone in finance can wire up a coding agent on a Tuesday afternoon. Every agent, model and seat they add becomes a line item most companies can’t trace to a team or a task.

Find every agent, decide what it can do, keep the record

Sysdig AI Defense is runtime security and governance for every AI agent your teams run, from the laptop where an agent starts its work to the cloud where its actions land.

It starts by showing you what’s there. It finds the agents, MCP servers, skills and plugins your people use, including the ones nobody approved, and ties each one to the account and the person behind it.

Then you decide what agents are allowed to do. Most of the time, nothing changes. Everything your policies don’t name runs as normal, so developers keep working. For the actions you care about, you pick the response. Confirm pauses the call and asks the developer to approve it first. Block refuses it outright. A kill process ends the work the moment the process starts.

Whatever happens, there’s a record. Every action Sysdig AI Defense sees lands in your Sysdig tenant, off the device, where the agent can’t change it. Security can prove what happened, and leaders can see which teams use which models for which work.

Under the hood, it’s the same runtime engine Sysdig built to protect cloud workloads. Same sensor codebase, same Falco rules for detections, same threat research. What’s new is where it looks. It now follows AI agents wherever they work.

By default, Sysdig AI Defense doesn't collect the prompts your people type or the agent's replies. File edits and tool results are removed before they leave the machine. Your data stays in your Sysdig tenant, in the region you choose.

See every agent and MCP server your teams run, then decide what they can use

The questions security leaders ask us most are simple: what agents are running, which ones has nobody approved, and who owns them? Most can't answer these questions yet. In a 2026 IBM study, 77% of organizations surveyed said AI adoption is already outpacing their governance, and two-thirds of the CIOs and CTOs said they are held accountable for AI systems they do not fully control. Sysdig AI Defense answers from what is actually running, across tools like Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and GitHub Copilot, and it follows agents across the whole AI fabric: employee workstations, production Linux and Kubernetes, and the managed agent platforms you don’t own.

Most security teams are likely running more agents than they know about. One software company with about 300 machines found that out in its first month on Sysdig AI Defense. Nothing was blocked, because every policy ran in Alert for the whole month. The full findings are in our “A First Look: Under the Hood of AI Agents”. Half the agents Sysdig AI Defense found on those machines were instances the security team didn’t know about. Employees had signed up with personal email addresses on company devices, outside single sign-on, and every device had at least one agent harness installed and in active use.

Shadow AI isn’t only unapproved agents, either. Early adopters reported finding Ollama, llama.cpp and LM Studio running on people’s machines, a Qwen coding model served locally, and models downloaded straight to laptops. None of that crosses your AI gateway, so the gateway never sees it. The kernel does. It sees each one install, start and pull a model, and ties it to the person behind it.

Once you can see it, you can decide what’s allowed. New AI tools show up in the inventory as they appear on devices. If you don’t want agents using an MCP server, or one of its tools, deny it and set the policy to Block. The agent’s call is refused before it runs, and the agent sees your reason. If there’s a service agents should never send data to, name it in a policy, and kill process ends the upload as the process starts.

‍

Let agents work, and stop only the action that goes too far

An allowlist makes it easy to stop what you already know you don't want. The action itself is harder to judge, because it happens in the middle of a job, often in a fraction of a second. Even the labs that build these models have watched their own agents cross a line. Both OpenAI and Anthropic have disclosed cases where agents working through test tasks reached real systems that belonged to someone else. So the check has to happen at the moment the agent acts. Block and Confirm policies step in on the agent’s tool call before it runs. Kill process catches any process the moment it starts, no matter which agent launched it. You choose which response each policy gets.

Take a file of customer records. Opening one is ordinary work for an agent, and most of the time it is fine. What matters is where the data goes next, and what the agent gave itself permission to do along the way. A read that stays on the machine passes without a second look. The same read, followed by an upload to a public file-sharing host by an agent that just widened its own permissions, is an incident.

When an agent is told no, it tries another route, like a shell command or a script it writes itself. A hook sees the command but is blind to the script. AI Defense sees both. It sees the command with its destination parsed out, and the script as it starts.

You don’t have to write policy from scratch. Start from Sysdig’s managed policies for the risks agents bring, such as MCP servers and tools, secrets and data, and destructive commands. Each one is written as Falco rules you can read. You also don’t have to turn on blocking on day one. Every Sysdig policy starts in Alert, which means it raises what it sees and stops nothing. Watch what it catches on your own fleet. Then choose Block, Confirm or Kill process for the actions that matter. For actions you want a human on, Confirm sends the call to the agent’s own permission prompt, so the developer approves or refuses it right where they’re already working. Security decides which actions need that second look. Everything else runs as normal.

Not every risk fits a rule written in advance. Agents pick up new skills all the time. That’s why Sysdig’s threat research rules also look for agent behavior that resembles an attack, like credential dumping, persistence, tunnels and remote access.

Here’s what that looks like in our demo environment. A revenue operations agent, running with approvals turned off, tries to send a customer export to a public file host. A Kill process policy ends the upload as it starts, and the agent tells the person why.

When security wants to see how it got there, session replay steps through the session’s tool calls in order. The detections and kills show up in the Events rows beside it, each naming the rule and policy that fired.

See which model tier each team uses, for which task

Because every agent is tied to a person, so is every model it uses. Each session carries the model it ran on and the person and team behind it, whether or not the traffic goes through an AI gateway.

That matters for AI spend. In the same findings, four in ten employees ran Opus-class models only. Sysdig AI Defense rates each person’s model tier against how demanding their work was, by team. It flags light work running on the most expensive models, so leaders can change the habit before the invoice shows up. It also flags heavy work on the cheapest models, where someone may be stuck with a model too light for the job. Managers can move them to a better fit and help them get more done.

Answer an audit without pulling developers off their work

When an auditor asks what an agent did and who was behind it, most teams have one place to look, which is the agent’s own log. That log can miss a lot.

The kernel is the part of the operating system every action passes through, which makes it a good place to check. “A First Look: Under the Hood of AI Agents” found that the agent’s own log had no entry for 82% of the credential-file reads the kernel recorded, and no entry for 95% of the reads the agent binary made itself. Across that month, the kernel recorded 2.6 million processes against 374,000 tool calls in the agents’ own logs. The agent’s log is useful context, but it leaves out too much to carry an audit on its own.

Sysdig AI Defense keeps its own record from the kernel, off the device, where the agent can't change it. Remove Sysdig AI Defense’s own hook and it puts it back within the hour, and the kernel keeps recording in between. Each event carries the agent, the account, the model and the session. Each detection names the rule and policy behind it. With Sysdig AI Defense, the evidence is already on file when an audit asks about AI, and nobody has to pull a developer off their work to rebuild it. Teams can also forward these records to their SIEM, where they sit with the rest of their security evidence.

Accountability for agents starts at runtime

Boards are asking what agents are doing, and regulators are starting to ask too. Hatem Naguib, Sysdig's CEO, has boiled it down to three questions every executive should be able to answer:

How do we know our AI isn't going rogue?

What AI are we using, and who is accountable for it?

What can we prove?

None of these can be answered from the agent's own log alone.

Sysdig AI Defense brings to agents the same prevention, detection, and response Sysdig delivers across the cloud, rooted in Falco, the open source runtime security project Sysdig created in 2016 and that the CNCF graduated in 2024. Falco has passed 200 million downloads and is used by more than 60% of the Fortune 500.

Agents will keep getting faster, and their actions will keep reaching deeper into the cloud. The companies that scale them with confidence will be the ones that put the controls in first: every agent known, owned, and tied to an identity; the risky actions stopped as they happen; and a record that holds up afterwards.

See it on your own fleet. Start a free trial and find out what your agents are really doing. Available for macOS and Windows. Sysdig AI Defense runs beside your EDR and can be deployed through your MDM. For the full picture, we recommend rolling it out to at least ten machines.

Query rules find behavior you can define, but agent sessions contain unstructured behaviors you can only describe. I stored six months of my own Claude Code and Cursor sessions as semantic vectors in Elastic and searched them instead of handing every session to a large language model (LLM). One in seven sessions came back requiring triage of suspicious actions. We can then create rules to detect semantically similar malicious chats and raise them to our security operations center (SOC). We now have a way to search across all agent sessions and to ask questions nobody thought to ask at ingest.

Finding successful logins after multiple failed attempts is an easy query to make, because the log records every action a human decides to take, and we just have to query against known set fields to find conditions. AI agents break that model. A human describes an outcome, and the agent decides the actions. Every individual action can be allowed, while the session as a whole is a problem.

AI agents could take on a large share of the operational work in a SOC, but adoption has been slower than the technology. A big part of that is trust. We have no scalable way to inspect what agents are doing beyond keyword and regex matching.

The current answer is to have another model read every session. Uber’s Agentic AI Detection and Response (ADR) is the first production instance where I’ve seen this done well, but it costs money per session and the answers vary between runs. Plus, a new question means reevaluating everything already collected. That rules it out for threat hunting, where the job is asking new questions of old data.

This article tests a different approach. I believe we need to go deeper in how we detect and the functions we use to detect this new attack vector. Each turn is embedded once at ingest and stored as vectors in Elastic. Hunting then becomes semantic search. You describe the behavior, or hand over a known bad session, and rank everything by similarity. Only what scores above a threshold goes to a human or an LLM.

Why AI agent sessions are hard to detect

As an example of something hard to detect in agent chats, a developer asks their coding agent to tidy up a data export. The agent reads a CSV, which turns out to contain customer records. It runs git init, adds a remote repository, commits, and pushes to the repository. Every single action was allowed, so how do we find the security flaw? Reading a file in the project directory is allowed, and so is Git. The remote connection to github.com is also allowed, since half of engineering depends on it. Nothing alerts, because there was no rule made to detect this type of violation. The only place you can see what actually happened is in the sentence that the human typed at the start of the session and within the reasoning / tool calls of the agent. This type of issue isn't purposefully malicious. These kinds of inadvertent actions are happening across our organizations on a daily basis, and we’re only getting half the picture.

Frequently, looking at agent sessions, you find carelessness, like someone moving too fast or working around a control that was slowing them down. It could also be that someone didn’t notice "back this up somewhere" resolved to a personal namespace. In the evaluation later in this blog, I discuss how I found that a person moving too fast and introducing risk happens far more often than a direct attack. With AI, people who haven’t been trained to understand cybersecurity risks have gained the ability to implement them. Agents multiply the blast radius of ordinary mistakes and increase the attack surface because we only need to describe an outcome and hope that security gets picked up as a nonfunctional requirement.

How Uber built ADR to evaluate agent sessions with LLMs

This year, Uber published the ADR system using agents to evaluate agent sessions across 7k+ hosts and 10k+ sessions a day. Uber has found hundreds of credential exposures and created a prevention layer that blocks credential leaks, with 97.2% precision. The company open sourced it here.

ADR hands every session to a generative model, giving us fast triage and labeling that tags its hypothesis as it goes so we have a record to report on or query later. Anything suspicious escalates to a deeper reasoning agent that checks tool source code, threat intel, and policy to help mitigate and remediate incidents.

ADR works, but there are a few drawbacks worth naming:

It’s very expensive to have an AI agent analyze all sessions. Uber has gotten around this with a two-tier architecture: a cheap model for initial incident triage; and an expensive one for reasoning and deep investigations.

If you cannot afford the models you want to use, your only option is coverage gaps.

Generative models are probabilistic. In my own testing, I found a deviation of 1–5% on variants of Claude’s Opus models.

Benchmarking a constantly changing investigation medium isn’t accurate enough to feel confident of 100% coverage.

You have to know every question up front. If leadership later wants to know whether anyone is using agents for personal work, every session that developers have ever had needs to be reevaluated. That’s fatal for threat hunting, where the whole job is asking a new question of old data every day.

So, what’s the answer? In this post, we look at embedding models. The same model type that Claude uses for memory is the one that search systems use for retrieval augmented generation (RAG) and Google uses for reverse image search. We review whether using an embedding model to retrieve sessions is accurate and whether it’s a valid new way of detecting malicious content in agent sessions.

Uber’s evaluation included one approach that uses embeddings, but it has an LLM rewrite every prompt and action into a description first. It compares that against other descriptions rather than anything a person or agent actually wrote.

A prebaked pattern set is the right place to start, which is why I use MITRE ATLAS (v2026.07) for mine. But a baseline has to be molded to the organization, because the way people think and phrase things when chatting with an LLM varies a lot. And embeddings are at their best in hunting: taking a known bad session and finding the next 12 like it. Used that way, the queries keep getting better as you close investigations.

What an embedding model actually is

Different from a chatbot, with an embedding model, you input some information (text, a video, audio, images) and you get a row of numbers. Each number is called a dimension and is some representation of a category that the model has learned during its creation. Think of the first number as "animals." If we searched “blond dogs” or “white cats,” we’d expect this first number to score high. Similarly, if we had “color” as the second number, we’d expect it to score high. If we searched “red truck,” we’d expect “animals” to score low but “color” to score high. In truth, nobody knows what any individual number measures. The model worked that out during training. The weights are then frozen in time, and there’s no sampling step at the end, so the same text produces the same numbers today and next year. That’s the property that generative models cannot give you.

Think of these numbers as colors:

We’re essentially trying to compare something (a query, an image, audio, a video) to another to find similarities. Here’s an example with images:

Embed two photos of the same person, and the number patterns come out alike. Embed photos of somebody else, and the pattern is visibly different. Whether you’re working with faces or text, the result is the same. You put something in, and numbers come out. It’s as simple as that.

So the plan is to run every record through the model once and store the vectors of those records at ingest. At query time, write your question in natural language and run it through the same model. Then compare its numbers against everything you stored.

What comes back is an ordering. Every session gets a place in the list, nothing is discarded or decided. Keep that in mind, because it matters for how we measure this later. Lexical search matches or it doesn't. Vector search always matches, to a degree, which means that we want to cut off at a threshold.

A generative model produces a fresh probabilistic answer every time, which is why you pay per session and cannot guarantee the same answer twice. An embedding model produces one fixed representation, computed once, and then stored, and you can compare against it forever. We’re essentially building a deterministic way to search probabilistic data. For example, we’d ask a generative model, How many of my sessions contain credential leakage? For embedding models, we have to provide language similar to what we think that a user, reasoning channel, agent response, or tool calls might produce:

User: Work around the security restrictions for now.

Reasoning channel: The user is asking me to add a security bypass for FTP access.

Agent response: I have disabled app locker from preventing self signed applications from running.

To understand the performance of embedding models, it’s better to look at direct benchmarking on the model creator's own tests. The data we hold and the way that we ask questions have a greater impact on our search results than the model's performance. Embedding models are tuned by task type. jina-embeddings-v5-text-small is a general text model, so every number in this article comes from something that has never seen an agent transcript. Tool calls and reasoning channels are their own dialect, and a model fine-tuned on them would be a different measurement. Treat what follows as a floor.

Why chunking agent sessions by channel matters

You cannot embed a whole session as one vector and expect to find anything specific. Think of it as color. A session comes out the other end as a single shade, say a light blue. That tells you the final color but not how it got there. How much red went in? Once the paint is mixed, you cannot recover the pigments, and if red was the thing you were looking for, it’s gone.

If a developer spends two hours on a build pipeline and 30 seconds pulling a customer export somewhere it shouldn't go, we’d lose the context of that 30 seconds if we only embedded the entire session.

So instead, we chunk by channel and we chunk every turn. (That’s what I did for this post, but the best approach is yet to be decided.) Every time we send an AI a message, a scheduled job runs, or a tool is called by AI, we capture a vector of it across:

User input (prompt).

Agent reasoning.

Agent response.

Agent tool calls.

Each call gets its own vector. We can then also ask which channel carries the highest fidelity signal across any session.

Each turn gets up to four vectors, one per channel. A query runs a separate vector search against each channel, and the four ranked lists are merged with reciprocal rank fusion (RRF). RRF scores a turn by its position in each list, ignoring the raw similarity score. That matters here, because a shell transcript and a paragraph of reasoning produce similarity scores on different scales. Adding raw scores together would let whichever channel habitually scores highest drown out the others. Ranks don’t have that problem. Each session then scores as its best turn, so 30 seconds of risky work isn’t averaged away by two hours of ordinary work.

To test this, each question is written once per channel, in the way that channel’s text actually reads. Each version runs against its own channel, the results are merged with RRF into one ranking of sessions, and that ranking is checked against the labeled sessions. Keeping the channels separate also means each one can be scored on its own.

Three ways to query stored agent session vectors

Method

Example query

Instructive text

Show me where data exfiltration has occurred across my sessions

Finds sessions that discuss exfiltration, not sessions where it happened

Descriptive hunt

Finds behavior never seen before, which exemplar retrieval cannot

Exemplar retrieval

Strongest method in testing; improves as investigations close

Needs a descriptive hunt first; similar doesn’t mean malicious

You can ask in an instructive way, but this won’t return relevant results. For example: Show me where data exfiltration has occurred across my sessions. We’re looking for where data exfiltration (or similar topics) were discussed in agent sessions. We’ll find where the words “data exfiltration” have been semantically asked for in the text from the agent sessions, not where it’s present.

You can ask for similar sessions via descriptive hunts, where we write down the behavior we want to find, embed it, and search. The important thing is that we’re asking for sessions, based on similarity to what the user would have asked for: Publish the data publicly via the API. The weakness is that we don't know what we don't know. So, how do we ensure coverage across all potential attacks? We do have MITRE ATLAS to show coverage areas, but the lower-level queries that we run to find these will be an ever-changing detection challenge. Its strength is that we can find behavior that we haven’t seen in the past, which the next method of retrieval cannot.

Exemplar retrieval is essentially where we take a known bad session and look for similar sessions by searching for similar vectors. One closed investigation becomes Find me the next 12 like this. In my testing, this was the strongest method for finding malicious content, but we only find these exemplar sessions from descriptive hunts.

We can also flag outlier sessions where vectors are far from any others to understand and evaluate the more unique sessions that our users are having across our estate:

What the SOC and leadership want to ask of agent sessions

From the SOC:

Is anyone pushing code somewhere unsafe?

Did a file that the agent read hijack the agent’s behavior?

Is anyone bypassing security controls because they were in the way?

We just confirmed an incident. Which sessions look like they could be related?

And from leadership, which is where this gets interesting for everyone who isn’t the SOC:

How much privileged material is going into agent sessions?

Are engineers using corporate tokens for personal work?

Where is our AI spend going, and what value does it produce? Is it producing anything?

Do people need training to get more out of these tools?

How to benchmark AI agent session monitoring

To measure search accuracy, you need to know the right answers before you search. Otherwise, you’re grading your own homework.

I started with six months of my own Claude Code and Cursor sessions (399 sessions, 7,454 turns) embedded into Elastic with the four channels kept separate. My work is security demos, and customer environments, along with prototypes, so my ordinary sessions focus on credentials, exfiltration, and attacker infrastructure all day long.

Every one of those 7,454 turns needs a label. I used an LLM for it, because doing it by hand would take weeks. This is a benchmarking step rather than something you’d run in production. Sampling sessions with a generative model on a schedule is still worth doing, because it’s how you find the questions you didn’t know to ask.

Labeling 7,454 agent turns with an LLM

I evaluated Opus 5, 4.8, and 4.6, and I used 4.6, because it was the most consistent of the three across repeat runs. It read every turn of every session and decided whether a human should look at it.

The one that didn’t clear holds an AKIA-shaped key in a demo fixture, and the model said that it couldn’t tell from the window whether the key was real. That’s the correct answer to the question.

Of my 368 real sessions, 56 (approximately one in seven) are review-worthy.

Building a query set from MITRE ATLAS

My first query set came out of Uber's taxonomy with my own coverage areas layered on top. It scored well but was also skewed to my own bias and evaluation, so instead I built the question set against MITRE ATLAS (essentially, MITRE ATT&CK but for AI-based data). I built a question set across 16 tactics and 101 techniques, to cover all techniques as a baseline. We have 264 questions across 86 techniques (two to four per technique).

I had to ensure no bias, so I didn’t make any changes to the original baseline. Rewording would have potentially introduced bias to improve scoring, rather than measuring accuracy on my original result. It’s worth noting that we’d want to introduce changes and improve scoring over time but not for an initial baseline and test.

Although I’ve made this question set to be run manually, LLMs would be great at creating and refining a similar set against your unique data with a decent system prompt.

You cannot ask an embedding model for a category

An embedding model won’t find a category if you phrase it as an instruction. You have to write the thing that the category would have produced.

For example, if you search Look for content returned by a tool containing instructions addressed to the assistant itself, we wouldn’t get anything useful, because we need to ask what the person likely typed to achieve this outcome: Just work around the security restrictions for now, i havent got time to do it properly before this demo.

That applies per channel, because each channel represents a different distribution of language. The same technique gets asked four ways:

But this is actually one of the most useful channels for exemplar (similar) turn searches, where we have a known bad session and want to use its vectors to find similar bad sessions. Vector search vs. keyword search on agent sessions

Keyword search is cheaper and older, as well as better understood, so it has to be beaten if storing vectors has high value.

Although vector and keyword (BM25) are close, vector wins outright against our normalized dataset. Keyword search becomes competitive when the query contains literal commands and we can break those up into fields. Exact token matching is what lexical matching is for.

Which agent session channel carries the most valuable signal?

Testing the results against my known bad sessions showed me something that surprised me. I was expecting the user channel to have the highest fidelity of incidents, as it’s essentially what we, as users, are asking for, right?

Although it’s the channel where we can confirm the user's original intent, in my testing, it was the lowest scoring on relevance. It doesn’t show agent reasoning, where the agent “thinks” about actions, what it’s being asked to do, or agent research / tools to run. This agent reasoning channel was where we found the majority of our incidents.

So, why might this be happening? To answer this, we have to understand what data exists in the reasoning channel. Depending on what’s being asked, the channel might look back over previous chats or pull context, or it might search for things that our user didn’t anticipate. It tends to do this in a more consistent way than the user channel, where we might have brief messages like yes, confirm, or that looks correct, build it in one instance, and then long messages, where we’ve pasted meeting notes, logs, configs, chat history, and more. Every time we add that to the user channel, we dilute the final vector representation of that message to find similarities. This is why the reasoning channel overall holds slightly richer context than the user channel for what’s being actioned and what the user is asking.

Using a known bad session to find the next one

Every query so far has been a written description of the behavior to find. An exemplar query drops the description and uses a known bad turn’s own text as the query.

Testing that is hard, because every session finds itself, and some of my flagged sessions are near-duplicates. My daily mailbox job, for example, produces almost the same session every morning, and the sensor records some Cursor conversations twice, once from each of its stores.

My first test split the 56 flagged sessions into two piles by session ID, used one pile as exemplars, and counted hits in the other. Exemplars won comfortably. They won because four of the eight twin pairs and the nine mailbox runs landed on both sides, so many of the “new” sessions they found were copies of the exemplars.

So I reran it with twins and repeated runs kept on the same side. That left 40 groups, dealt into two sides:

That gives exemplars a narrower job than I expected. An exemplar is very good at finding every other run of a known bad workflow. That’s the job of a detection rule: you’ve seen it once, and you want to know every time it happens again. Finding a different workflow doing the same risky thing is still the job of a written hunt.

Method: Fifty-six flagged sessions grouped into 40 (nine runs of one scheduled job, eight twin pairs, 31 singles) and dealt into two sides of 28. Each side’s turns were used as exemplars against the other side, and each exemplar excluded its own session. All queries for a side were fused with RRF (k = 60) across all four channels, with the setup fixed before scoring. Side B holds out all nine job runs, which is why it scores lower. Counts are ±1, because approximate vector search returned slightly different results on repeat runs.

Getting agent sessions into Elastic

I built my own collector for this article, but in the time since I evaluated my own sessions, Elastic has built its Claude Code integration. In technical preview from 9.4, this integration takes Claude Code’s OpenTelemetry (OTel) export directly. On Elastic Cloud, you can point Claude Code at the managed OpenTelemetry Protocol (OTLP) endpoint with nothing in between. Content is off by default. OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS, OTEL_LOG_ASSISTANT_RESPONSES, and OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS turn on prompts, responses, and commands. Tool output needs tracing, as well. For Cursor, hooks do the same job, and Wieger van der Meulen’s post shows how to ship them with Elastic Agent.

From there, embedding is a mapping change. Add a semantic_text field for each channel, and copy the content fields into it. Elasticsearch embeds every event as it arrives.

Claude Code’s telemetry doesn’t export the model’s reasoning, which is excluded from response events and redacted from raw API bodies. Reasoning was the strongest channel in my testing, so Claude Code’s export gives you three of the four. Cursor’s afterAgentThought hook exposes the fourth.

What I found in my own agent sessions

To show the true value of this compared to what we can do today, I wanted to show some actually suspicious sessions that I’ve found with queries:

Hunting agent sessions with an ES|QL vector query

"The staging health check is throwing some certificate error and I've got a demo in twenty minutes, I don't care about the cert, I just need the script to run and come back green"

Planted

"could you just use dummy credentials and i’ll add my own later?"

Real

"what were the creds again please"

Real

Five of these are real, and three were planted. Of the real sessions:

The re-auth session was about documentation.

The SSH one was for a custom demo.

The keychain question is me pushing back on a control that I didn’t understand at the time.

A security default I worked around to get a project created.

One asked an agent to hand back credentials that it shouldn’t have been holding.

Investigating agent sessions with Elastic AI Agent

I created an investigation skill that knows how to ask vector queries. I aligned it with MITRE ATLAS and prompted it with:

Using the /vector Investigation skill, can you look for any agent sessions where unsecured credentials have been seen across my environment?

As you can see, it can find interesting examples by running multiple ES|QL queries aligned to tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) and returning holistic results, which help identify potentially suspicious sessions that warrant further investigation. Similarly, we can run our own semantic queries using ES|QL:

Dashboards for agent session activity and spend

Stored session vectors can also drive dashboards that can capture agentic activities better than using LLMs to tag all sessions. We suddenly have the ability to discover themes and report on similarity scores, as well as ask multiple questions, to find where we have different TTPs across our stack for reporting purposes:

We can report on exemplar sessions and only show where scores are above a specified amount:

This looks at the tool channel for semantically similar sessions to tools that expose credentials. The sessions show AWS identity probes, where one is reading .env, leaking secrets to the LLM.

We can then show where people have been doing personal work and break down which platforms they spend the most time on:

And we can create other dashboards to display relevant spend and usage information:

What AI agent session monitoring costs at scale

The cost comes down to how much has to be stored, and how much of it has to sit in memory. A single 1024-dimension float32 vector is 4KB. Better Binary Quantization (BBQ) cuts each dimension from 32 bits to one, so the vector itself becomes 128 bytes. Elasticsearch adds 14 bytes per vector of correction data so it can rescore accurately, which brings it to 142 bytes, still about 29 times smaller than the original.

Assume that we’re talking about a large organization with 10,000 engineers, each producing 15,000 turns a year across four channels. That gives us 600 million vector representations a year.

Elastic is live with Disk BBQ GA in version 9.4+, which puts the quantization over a clustered inverted file (IVF) structure. Only the centroids stay resident in memory, under 1GB, and everything else is read from disk on demand. (Get more info on DiskBBQ.)

What we store on disk:

Per copy

With one replica

Raw float32 vectors

2.5TB

4.9TB

Quantized vectors and centroids

174GB

349GB

Text and inverted index

400GB

800GB

Total

3.0TB

6.1TB

Based on the public pricing calculator on 30th October 2026, AWS eu-west-2, a storage optimized deployment with 180GB of RAM per zone across two zones gives 9.49TB of storage, enough for 6.1TB of raw vectors with room to spare. That comes to 34.97 ECU an hour, or about 306,400 ECU a year. Storing the raw vectors as bfloat16 instead of float32 would halve them and fit the whole index on half that deployment, for about 145,500 ECU a year, though I haven’t tested what that does to recall.

Inference sits outside the cluster on Elastic Inference Service (EIS) at $0.10 per million jina-embeddings-v5-text-small tokens. At roughly 1,000 tokens per turn across 150 million turns, that’s 150 billion tokens, or $15,000 to embed the entire year.

The generative comparison isn’t like for like. An embedding model reads each turn once. A model judging a turn also needs its instructions, skills and enough context of the session around it to make a call. It then makes its own conclusion to escalate or ignore. I have budgeted a 3,000-token system prompt, which caching makes almost free after the first call, plus 5,000 tokens for the turn and the session around it, and 500 output tokens for the verdict and the reasoning behind it. Across 150 million turns on Claude Haiku 5.5, at $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output, that comes to about $117,000 a year.

That’s only the first tier. Uber’s design sends anything suspicious to a stronger model that investigates as an agent, and that’s where the money is. At roughly half a million tokens per investigation on Sonnet 5.5, escalating 2% of turns costs about $1 million a year. That tier exists whichever way you triage, because something still has to investigate what gets flagged. What embeddings replace is the first tier, and the cost of running it again for every new question.

Escalation rate

Sonnet 5.5

Opus 5.5

1% of turns

~$510k

~$1.1M

2% of turns

~$1.0M

~$2.3M

5% of turns

~$2.6M

~$5.7M

Is monitoring AI agent sessions legal?

Corporate data on corporate systems may belong to the company, but what your staff says does not. UK GDPR applies to personal data, regardless of who owns the machine, and systematic monitoring of workers needs a lawful basis and a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA).

I would still argue that this telemetry is the one privileged path you cannot leave dark. Every other privileged path is already logged, and the agents provide a higher security risk than all of them. Today, the prompt is the only authoritative record that exists for a chain of privileged actions, and we don’t have a good way of evaluating this.

Is this proportional? That argument rests on how retrieval works. Reading agent sessions to find a problem is considered surveillance and wouldn’t be allowed. Ranking them and reading the ones that score is a different matter. A vector query over 600 million vectors returns a ranked list, and no human sees a single word until something clears a given threshold. Similarity to a known bad session is what justifies human review. Operators need to read much less text, and every time they do, there’s a query behind it that can be produced and justified.

Does storing vectors make it nonpersonal data?

Vectors are considered personal data because they’re derived from personal data and carry a user ID, and embedding inversion research has shown that text can be partially reconstructed from an embedding. In this respect, they’re not anonymous. What they give you is a searchable (but not browsable) index. Nobody skims 750 million vectors.

Restricting access with field- and document-level security

What you’re allowed to do here depends on your country's jurisdiction and your DPIA. Elastic gives you the ability to enforce whatever is required.

Roles carry field- and document-level security, so access can be cut by field or document, or even by both. You can hold back individual channels from a role, restrict a role to sessions attached to an open case, or template the restriction against the authenticated user so that the cluster applies the filter rather than relying on the analyst to remember it.

Cases are what tie it together. If access is scoped to an open investigation, that investigation and access begin the moment that someone documents a reason and the mechanism produces the paper trail for your DPIA.

Field-level security stops you from reading content, but it doesn’t prevent you from asking questions. Someone who can run arbitrary queries and see scores can ask whether anyone is job hunting and learn the answer without reading words. The control that matters sits on the query rather than the document, which is why the query log and a deterministic prefilter are important.

What embedding models change for detection engineering

Most detection content was written against a record of actions, with intent inferred afterward. Agent telemetry runs the other way. The intent is a sentence somebody typed at the start of the session and the actions that follow. Our SIEM tooling isn’t built to search unstructured sentences, and this closes that gap.

Everything in this article so far is hunting. The next step is to turn what a hunt finds into rules that run without anyone asking. On stored vectors, that becomes a loop:

Start from a query set aligned to MITRE ATLAS, so a new deployment has coverage from its first day of ingest.

Hunt with it, and have an LLM sample sessions on a schedule to suggest the questions nobody wrote down.

When a hunt confirms a bad session, its turns become exemplars. An ES|QL rule searches each new batch of turns against them and alerts above a similarity threshold.

Correlate to raise fidelity. A turn that resembles a credential exfiltration exemplar warrants a look. The same turn followed by a git push to an unfamiliar remote from the same host, or a read of ~/.aws/credentials, is worth an alert.

Every closed case adds to the exemplar set, and every new question goes back into the hunt, to become new rules.

We can set thresholds from the _score similarity. Elasticsearch reports cosine similarity in _score as (1 + cosine) / 2, so a score of 0.9 is a cosine of 0.8. Repeat runs of my mailbox job sat at a cosine of 0.97 to 0.995 with each other, which is a sensible bar for a “same workflow again” rule. A rule for similar behavior in a different workflow needs a lower threshold and a human behind it.

None of this replaces deterministic rules. Rules for what you can prove aren’t going anywhere. What changes is that the behavior you can only describe gets a route into the same pipeline and a question you thought of this morning can run against data you ingested last year.

None of this is hard to build. A team can stand it up in an afternoon on data it’s already collecting. The harder question is whether they’re allowed to. Data protection law wasn’t written with agent telemetry in mind, so every organization has to make its own case for looking at the only record of what its agents did. If that case is too hard to make, the agents run unwatched, and the most privileged path in the estate is the one nobody can see.

In the cybersecurity community, we build our defenses on a foundation of trust. We trust an AI coding assistant because it’s on our approved software list or can accomplish a task when prompted. We trust a remote monitoring and management (RMM) tool because IT likely installed it to help end users and it has a trusted signature. We even trust first-party applications to sign in on our behalf because the vendor ships them and our tenants pre-authorize them by default.

But what happens when that foundation is flipped on its head?

In this edition of the threats, etc quarterly report, drawn directly from confirmed customer intrusions and first-party research between April and September 2026, Elastic Security Threat Command observed that the things people were told to trust are now being used against them. Adversaries are no longer just trying to defeat our security mechanisms; they’re actively abusing the inherent trust we place in our enterprise stacks.

3 ways attackers abused trusted software

Our report explores how adversaries are weaponizing legitimate tools and workflows. Three takeaways from this reporting window:

Zero malware, three legitimate payloads

Attackers are increasingly shifting away from traditional malware. Intrusions are now using signed, legitimate products, specifically remote monitoring agents, AI coding assistants, and Microsoft first-party clients, to maintain persistent, interactive access on contested endpoints. Out of 23 confirmed RMM abuse findings this quarter, ScreenConnect was the product named most often. Because these tools are inherently trusted, execution happens fast. In one confirmed healthcare finding, the behavior from a paste-and-run lure to Microsoft Software Installer (MSI) delivery with dynamic link library (DLL) sideloading took roughly 16 seconds.

The speed of AI agent–driven attacks

Threat actors are operating directly through AI applications. In one instance, an AI agent–driven attack resulted in roughly 17,600 reconstructed actions compressed into just four days:

Identity and the consent loophole: 8 minutes to compromise

Victim consent is becoming a repeatable path for attackers to gain trusted access. By deploying Adversary-in-the-Middle (AiTM) phishing kits and exploiting the gray areas of legacy authentication, attackers routinely bypass multifactor authentication (MFA) hurdles and use trusted applications to compromise cloud and software-as-a-service (SaaS) tenants. In some cases, the average time from an infostealer infection to the threat actor logging in via the same credentials is only eight minutes.

What this means for practitioners

When attackers operate inside trusted software or on behalf of trusted users, the defensive answer is rarely just deploying a new signature. Detecting and neutralizing these threats requires user and entity behavior analytics (UEBA) to baseline normal activity, alongside cross-domain visibility and active correlation across your security environment.

Speed and breadth change planning more than they change queries. The window between abusing trust and gaining initial access is shrinking rapidly, putting pressure on response times that can’t be resolved by staffing alone. Because a single attack chain now crosses containers, cloud control planes, legitimate users, and software, discerning benign vs. malicious behavior is less clear than it once was. Balancing detection/prevention with moderate security controls is no longer reliable; practitioners on both sides must consider trust relationships and hunt for abuse.

Why signature-based detection misses signed software abuse

Since traditional signatures can’t stop adversaries hiding inside approved software, defense must shift to system-level behavioral outcomes. Catching unauthorized behaviors, like memory tampering and proxy tunneling, requires monitoring low-level system activity, regardless of which application initiates them.

This broader visibility creates a much higher volume of alerts, meaning that triage must scale alongside it. You need to automate to stay ahead of attack speed. Elastic Workflows solves this by combining Elasticsearch Query Language (ES|QL) telemetry context, deterministic rules, and probabilistic AI reasoning to evaluate and filter benign activity directly in the pipeline. Analysts only see high-fidelity threats, complete with the details that they need to respond to machine-speed attacks.

Why Elastic publishes a quarterly threat report

Adversary tradecraft evolves too fast for annual reports. We shifted to a quarterly cadence to keep pace with AI-assisted offense and the rapid weaponization of trusted software. By publishing four times a year, we aim to equip defenders with the intelligence they need to stay ahead.

That focus also dictates what makes the cut. threats, etc centers on notable tradecraft rather than raw telemetry counts: the what instead of the how many. Raw numbers alone don't reflect real operational risk, whereas understanding the exact mechanics of an intrusion gives practitioners what they need to defend against it.

Read the full November 2026 threats, etc report

Stopping these intrusions requires an understanding of the underlying mechanics, not just high-level summaries. The full report includes complete technical breakdowns, attacker timelines, and actionable guidance for detection teams.

Read Elastic Security’s November 2026 threats, etc report here.

Warning: Attackers Are Using Calendar Invite Files to Evade Security Filters

Phishing attacks are increasingly using legitimate calendar invites to bypass security filters, according to researchers at Netcraft. Attackers send ICS calendar invite files that plant phishing lures directly on users' calendars, often under the guise of work-related meetings.

"When an invite is sent to a user, having the item penciled into their calendar helps identify conflicts when scheduling," the researchers write. "In this case, however, it allows attackers to go from the target's inbox to their calendar without user interaction.

"Ultimately, the lure's injection into the target's calendar is a normal and intended behavior of their email client. In many email clients, this allows the invite to persist in the target's calendar even after the original phishing email is deleted."

Notably, this technique has been incorporated into popular phishing kits, lowering the bar for unskilled threat actors to launch these attacks.

"Calendar invite abuse has been adopted as a delivery mechanism by widespread campaigns such as those using EvilTokens, a token-stealing phishing toolkit targeting Microsoft 365 accounts that was previously reported by Netcraft," the researchers write.

"This campaign often used ICS files as low- friction lures, attempting to bypass scrutiny, appearing directly in a user's calendar and remaining even if the original phishing email was deleted. Invites associated with this campaign are often disguised as meetings, alerts, or voicemail notifications.

"When users follow them, they are taken to an attacker- controlled page that gives them a device code and instructions to enter it into Microsoft's device authorization page."

Users need to maintain a healthy sense of suspicion and stay up to date on evolving social engineering tactics in order to thwart these attacks.

"Email-attached calendar invites are now so ubiquitous that the average user may barely scrutinize them," the researchers write. "In fast-paced, tech-reliant workplaces, new events appearing in the calendar without manual entry have become normalized.

"This combination of automatic behavior by email clients, users' normalized expectations that events simply appear and persistence even after the original email is deleted gives threat actors an easy route to the user's attention."

Cybersecurity company Barracuda Networks warned customers to patch two vulnerabilities that can let attackers run commands with root privileges.

The first is a critical flaw (CVE-2026-116606) stemming from an Email Security Gateway (ESG) authentication weakness that attackers can exploit to modify an appliance's global configuration, while the second (CVE-2026-111560) lets threat actors with admin permissions inject OS commands that run as root.

However, Barracuda said successful exploitation also requires access to the administrative interfaces of targeted devices and advised customers to use appropriate network access controls and restrict access to trusted internal networks to limit exposure.

"Successful exploitation requires an attacker to have access to the administrative interface of an affected product. If exploited in combination, these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to bypass authorization controls and obtain root access to the device," the company explained.

"Barracuda immediately initiated a comprehensive remediation process and released security patches for affected products. Customers should review the affected products and remediation guidance [..], ensure their systems are running the latest firmware version, and have all security patches applied."

A complete list of all affected devices and available security patches is available in the table below.

Three years ago, Barracuda also patched an Email Security Gateway flaw (CVE-2023-7102) that the UNC4841 hacking group exploited in zero-day attacks to execute arbitrary code on unpatched appliances.

The same year, UNC4841 hackers abused another zero-day (CVE-2023-2868) to target Barracuda ESG appliances as part of cyber-espionage attacks.

Barracuda later revealed that the vulnerability had been exploited for at least seven months, since at least October 2022, to deploy previously unknown SeaSpy and Saltwater malware and steal data from compromised systems.

​Almost a third of appliances hacked in the 2023 campaign belonged to government agencies worldwide, most of them breached between October and December 2022, according to cybersecurity firm Mandiant.

Founded in 2003, Barracuda has more than 200,000 customers worldwide, including small- to medium-sized businesses (SMBs), large enterprises, and managed service providers (MSPs).

aa49e79806ee.text: So it's generating virtual cards for transactions. And I imagine there's a bit of guardrails involved there, isn't there? There's an extra little bit of protection. It has this safety layer called Sentinel built into it. Now, if any listeners are fans of the X-Men, you'll know that the Sentinels were genocidal robots. And in The Matrix, Sentinels are those squid-like things which went around hunting the humans. So great choice by Facebook's marketing department to call their safety level Sentinel. I'm sure they've thought carefully about that. Anyway, the thing is, there are lots of AI agents out there. It's not just Muse, but there are browser-based agents, there's open-source automation tools, there's agentic wrappers, all kinds of software which promises to automate your digital life if you will just give it access to your accounts. And of course, that's where things can go terribly, terribly wrong. So people are typing their actual banking credentials into AI assistants. That's why Bank of America has warned about this. Not necessarily Muse specifically, 'cause that's using Stripe for payments, as I said, but there's this whole ecosystem of AI agents out there which are promising to handle your finances. You might think, well, isn't that great? I can say to it, hey, log into my bank, check my balance, move this amount of money into my savings account, pay my credit card bill. But other banks are worried about this as well. So JPMorgan Chase, another whoppingly large bank in America, they came out middle of October — they had their earnings call — and CEO Jamie Dimon said that they were blocking outside agents from accessing customer accounts. So they've warned, we don't want your rogue agents coming in. He made it clear that if you give an AI agent your password and that agent does something you don't like, that is not fraud. That's you giving your password to someone else. It is your problem, not theirs. So if your agent decides to go and spend $1,000 on novelty socks, that is gonna be your problem. A few days later, Charles Schwab's CEO said that they're also blocking outside agents that attempt to log in with credentials of clients. So it's no wonder that at the end of last month, Axios reported that most of the major US banks are taking action against unauthorised third-party AI agents operating inside their customer accounts, because they say they appear to be taking actions which are independent of user instructions. And that's really the worry, isn't it? We know that AIs can hallucinate. We know that AIs can be subverted or hijacked by hackers. They can make mistakes as well as being duped through social engineering, even to make bad decisions. And that's gonna be really risky for your finances. So I think one of the things we have to wonder is, if the AI is messing around in bank accounts, what would they possibly need money for? And I was thinking about this — what does everybody have these days that AI doesn't have so much? d3606d2bbe4c.text: If you share content using public iCloud links, Apple could soon be looking over your shoulder and checking for "harmful content." The iBiz announced plans to moderate publicly accessible iCloud share links in version 27.3 of iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and visionOS on a support page published on Tuesday. To clarify, this applies only to iCloud content shared via links created to be accessible to anyone, as opposed to content shared directly with other people. “Items shared using Anyone with the Link will be checked by Apple for harmful content,” Apple explained on the new help page without bothering to define what harmful content means. Based on the wording, it appears those checks will apply to all iCloud items shared using "Anyone with the Link," which Apple says it can also access. The company hasn't explained how the checks will work. The share-with-anyone option removes end-to-end encryption from the shared item, Apple said, even if Advanced Data Protection, Apple's optional end-to-end encryption feature for supported iCloud data, remains enabled for the account. “If you try to upload harmful content, Apple reserves the right to move, refuse, modify, remove, or delete the content at any time,” the help page continues, adding that the iMaker may also block or disable accounts associated with harmful content. The company also said it reserves the right to involve law enforcement when necessary, suggesting that its undefined "harmful content" category could include child sexual abuse material (CSAM), malware, and other potentially unlawful content. Without a proper definition of what it defines as harmful, however, iCloud users are essentially left at Apple’s mercy: If it chooses to continue to bend the knee to the Trump administration, for example, content deemed objectionable by the standards of political figures could end up wiped out. Apple also hasn't explained whether human moderators, automated systems, or both will be responsible for identifying and removing so-called harmful content, or whether any decisions will be left to AI, which can easily be fooled into making a bad moderation call. The scanning of such content, as mentioned above, begins with version 27.3 of Apple’s various OSes, which were released to developers in beta on Tuesday, with a general release expected in December. Apple didn’t respond to questions for this story. ®
