The kinks in the software supply chain are once again being exposed, with attackers now targeting OpsShield’s update process.

This week, threat actors used compromised credentials to push malicious updates out to cPGuard customers. They then accessed data stored on the vendor’s servers and in its billing portal accounts, and made copies of at least three of OpsShield’s cloud servers.

The company said in an advisory that it has “shut the attacker out of every system we know they reached, and … are rebuilding the ones we cannot fully trust.” It has also released updates and urges customers to update to the latest version of cPGuard, change passwords, and generate new SSH keys.

Ultimately, the breadth of this unsanctioned access underscores the continued fragility of the software supply chain, as well as the vulnerability of security tools themselves.

“The real danger here is that attackers were able to turn a trusted security update mechanism into a vector to break into servers,” said Erik Avakian, a technical counselor at Infotech. “The software that’s supposed to protect those servers became the source that compromised them.”

The anatomy of the attack

OpsShield specializes in server protection and web security software. Its cPGuard product is a security suite, malware scanner, and firewall designed for Linux web hosting servers.

The company disclosed that, between November 1 and 2, attackers were able to gain unauthorized access to the OpsShield update distribution infrastructure, and, for about 70 minutes, pushed out a malicious update.

The threat actors began by probing OpsShield’s billing portal, registering a customer account under a false identity, and ordering a free cPGuard trial. They then sent crafted requests that allowed them to gain the ability to run commands on the server to collect data. They used stolen access keys to publish fake updates that ran as root (the highest level of admin privilege), and to copy sensitive files and make copies of three OpsShield cloud servers.

About 2,950 customer servers ran the fake update, exposing password hashes, root SSH keys, MySQL root passwords, and shell history, OpsShield reported. Attackers also accessed about 7,900 billing portal accounts containing customer names, addresses, emails, and hashed passwords.

OpsShield says it is still reviewing the exact request that provided access, and has patched two possible entry points and verified related vendor components “line by line.” It closed the attacker’s account, revoked the stolen update-storage key as well as “every cloud API token and access key on our account.”

The company also removed the attacker’s secure shell (SSH); deleted the clones of its servers created by the attacker plus any snapshots; turned on stronger login protection and replaced every SSH key and password; reset all billing portal login sessions and rotated all keys; and began rebuilding its billing, licensing, and internal management servers with tighter PHP and firewall settings.

The company has also published clean updates: v5.88.26, which removes the hidden root shell; plus a follow-up which removes the scheduled task left by the attacker. Further, it began re-issuing all cPGuard license private and public keys so that the copies the attacker gained access to stopped working.

The company advised admins to:

Update cPGuard to the latest version, then confirm that /etc/cron.d/i93677, /var/tmp/.i93677/ and /var/tmp/.cpg91511_sh are gone; delete them if not;

Change root passwords and every local user password on the server;

Generate new root SSH keys and remove old ones from every server that trusted them; until the keys are changed, treat the servers as compromised;

Change MySQL root passwords and any database passwords and rotate any password, API key, or token existing in root shell histories;

Reset the OpsShield billing portal passwords and turn on two-factor authentication.

Finally, it said, “if we told you the attacker logged in to your server by hand, rebuild it from a clean backup taken before 1 November.”

OpsShield being transparent, but the impacts are still real

“Frankly, few vendors write a breach disclosure this candid,” said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research. “OpsShield deserves a lot of credit for that.”

However, he pointed out, the worst kind of breach is the one a security tool delivers. Update channels are left unlocked on purpose, and security tools run as root because they have to see everything, “so the fake update ran as root too.”

For a hosting provider, one server can hold hundreds of customer websites and databases. A MySQL root password opens all of them, and a root SSH key grants access to every other server that trusts it. Shell history also often contains typed passwords and tokens.

The downstream customer may be hit hardest while knowing the least, Dickson pointed out, as most website owners have no idea which security agent their hosting provider runs. Every server that updates itself trusts the vendor’s pipeline.

OpsShield describes itself as a small team selling to smaller hosts at a low price, which is the uncomfortable truth of the supply chain, Dickson said. “Your exposure is set by the smallest vendor holding root on your servers, not the largest.”

Avakian agreed that this serves as a reminder that an enterprise’s software supply chain is only as secure as the systems, identities, and processes behind it. “You can do everything you can to secure your own infrastructure and still get compromised through a third-party supplier you trust.”

What’s particularly concerning here is that the attackers didn’t have to go after thousands of customers one by one; they only had to compromise a single distribution mechanism to turn the vendor’s own trusted infrastructure against its customers, he noted.

Third parties extend risk, which is a fact that organizations still underestimate, he said. “Enterprises need to pay much more attention to third-party and supply chain risk management.”

Zero-trust a must-have

Avakian also pointed out that the impact on downstream customers could go well beyond initial compromise, as stolen credentials can be used to carry out further attacks. Enterprises should take a zero-trust approach that includes their software suppliers and the updates they rely on.

“Just because an update comes from a trusted source doesn’t mean you can assume it’s safe,” he said. Enterprises should take a closer look at vendor risk, protect privileged credentials, and examine software integrity. Also, continuously monitor for unexpected behavior after an update and be ready to isolate systems quickly if and when something goes wrong.

“You have to plan for the possibility that even a trusted supplier can be compromised,” he emphasized. “And you need to practice those types of scenarios as part of a regular table-top exercise program.”

Dickson advised starting with an inventory, and knowing every vendor agent running with root or administrator privilege, as each one is an update channel. Customers should ask vendors where update publishing keys live and what separates them from customer-facing systems, watch outbound traffic from servers, keep secrets out of shell history, and treat SSH keys as credentials with an expiration date. Downstream customers should ask their host directly whether it runs cPGuard, then change their own passwords.

“The most dangerous software on your server may be the software you trust to update itself,” he said. “Choose those vendors as if they hold root, because they do.”

This article originally appeared on NetworkWorld.

Fortinet FortiOS and FortiProxy Authentication Bypass Vulnerability (CVE-2024-55591)

In February 2026, CrowdStrike Counter Adversary Operations identified an open directory controlled by the Iran-nexus adversary STATIC KITTEN on IP address 157.20.182[.]49 containing 1.9 GB of data and more than 20,000 files. Among them was a modified version (SHA256 hash: fd6b46d148af22da6163f18ce43b35ebb827cc6e140f03f0f514bc2a6f548743) of a public POC exploit for a FortiOS and FortiProxy authentication bypass vulnerability (CVE-2024-55591) first released by a well-known industry source on January 27, 2025.4

Where the public POC exploit executed a single user-provided command, the modified version contained 13 hardcoded payloads designed to enumerate targets, create users, and establish persistence. The modifications reflect a systematic approach to turning a demonstration tool into a more comprehensive exploit.

Table 1. Payloads for modified CVE-2024-55591 exploit

Payload Name

Description

test

Creates the backdoor admin user FortiWiFi with password FortiWiFi123 and assigns this user the super_admin profile, granting full system access

test2

Lists all user groups in the victim system, likely to facilitate reconnaissance in order to understand the victim system’s existing group structure

test3

Displays all local user accounts, allowing the attacker to enumerate existing users

test4

Modifies the FortiWiFi admin account by assigning it the ssl-vpn-groupamoss access profile

test5

Creates the FortiWiFi user with password FortiWiFi123, adds this user to the ssl-vpn-groupamoss group, and then displays all user groups to verify the user was successfully added to the group

test6

Creates or modifies a user group named ssl-vpa-amoss and adds multiple users to this group, including the backdoor FortiWiFi account (created by test1 or test5) and users with transliterated Hebrew-language names (i.e., shachar, sigal, amos, sima, lev, and gabi)

test7

Queries the ssl-vpn-groupamoss group configuration’s help information, likely to understand available options for follow-on activities

test8

Creates the backdoor user darlen with password 1234

test9

Similar to the test payload, creates the FortiWiFi user with password FortiWiFi123 or updates the existing FortiWiFi user to use that password

test10

Creates the FortiWiFi user with password 1234 and adds this user (along with numerous other users, many with transliterated Hebrew-language names) to the VPN-Users group, potentially to hide the backdoor account among legitimate users

test11

Creates a system admin account named FortiSetup with super_admin privileges and an encrypted password (decrypted password is gwm1607pmw); this account provides a more sophisticated backdoor than those created by other payloads, as FortiSetup has root VDOM access

test12

Displays the FortiAdmin account’s configuration, likely to facilitate reconnaissance

test13

Creates a user named offices with an email address and an encrypted password (decrypted password is @lolo@123456); POC_ZZ_1.py‘s developer may have added this email address to make the new user appear legitimate

Whether STATIC KITTEN modified the public CVE-2024-55591 exploit themselves or obtained this modified version from another source remains unknown. However, as of this writing, CrowdStrike Counter Adversary Operations has not observed any other adversaries using this modified POC or infrastructure hosting it.

AI’s Impact on the Vulnerability Research Ecosystem

AI advancements are undoubtedly accelerating the speed and scope of how vulnerabilities are discovered and weaponized.5 One only has to look at the substantial increase in the number of vulnerabilities in recent Microsoft Patch Tuesdays compared to prior to the advent of frontier models earlier this year.6

Detecting and attributing adversaries’ direct use of AI for vulnerability research purposes remains hard to identify due to inherent visibility gaps and the fact there is no single identifier that distinguishes AI-generated exploit code. Complicating things further, is that the patterns suggesting AI assistance (such as well-commented code, improvements to existing POCs, or structured code organization) are also consistent with the output of someone with high technical capabilities.

Nonetheless, threat actors are leveraging AI to augment their vulnerability research. CrowdStrike Intelligence assesses they will almost certainly continue to do so through at least three vectors:

Direct interaction with frontier models by trying to “jailbreak” AI safeguards and bypass any export control restrictions

Modifying open-weight proprietary models for malicious use by extracting safeguards; these are not/less monitored for abuse by frontier AI companies

Adopting AI-led/assisted public vulnerability research published by industry sources

The third point, while not a direct use, is the easiest to detect. One only has to look at the CopyFail vulnerability detailed in this blog post, whose discovery was allegedly facilitated by AI.7 Or the mass exploitation of wp2shell in July 2026, which is the first critical unauthenticated WordPress Core remote code execution (RCE) purportedly discovered in nearly a decade and was allegedly discovered using GPT5.6 Sol Ultra and $25 USD worth of tokens.8

Outlook

Adversaries will almost certainly continue using public vulnerability research as part of their offensive toolkit through the foreseeable future. As more POC exploits become routinely available within hours of disclosure, at least partially driven by AI-assisted vulnerability research, the number of threat actors using them will almost certainly increase. Over the next year, this will likely manifest itself in the rise of widespread exploitation campaigns resulting in contested environments, like the cPanel CVE-2026-41940 exploitation example covered in this blog post.

This expanding pool of adversaries leveraging public vulnerability research, combined with the rapid speed at which adversaries are operationalizing public research, reinforces three key points.

The first is that patch prioritization is harder than ever. As vulnerability disclosures continue to increase in volume, predicting which ones will attract public research (and therefore adversary attention) becomes a genuine intelligence challenge. Because adversaries have access to the same advisories and public exploits that defenders do, organizations that rely solely on CVSS scores to drive patching decisions are relying on the wrong signal. Real-world exploitability, ease of exploitation (i.e., if there is a public exploit or exploitation guidance), and adversary intent are what separate the vulnerabilities that matter from the ones that do not.

The second is that the time to patch is effectively zero. The data from the first half of 2026 shows this: 91% of vulnerabilities with POCs that CrowdStrike has seen exploited were weaponized and used in the wild within 48 hours, with the fastest observation occurring just 35 minutes after a POC became available. Adversaries treat public vulnerability research as the starting gun, and legacy patch cycles measured in weeks or days cannot compete.

Lastly, more threat actors can participate in exploitation. As the case studies show, adversaries across skill and resource levels are operationalizing public research, some using POCs with minimal modification and others refining them (as UMBRAL BISON and STATIC KITTEN both demonstrated). When motivation and intent are the only remaining barriers to exploitation, the volume of participating adversaries significantly increases.

The vulnerability research ecosystem is one of the security community's greatest assets and most significant challenges. Defenders who treat public research as a threat actor's green light, and who build the intelligence, patching timelines, and detection capabilities to match, are the ones who will keep pace.

Jaime Duque and Lacie Blythe are Senior Intelligence Analysts at CrowdStrike. This research was presented at Day Zero 2026.

How long does it take your security teams to detect a threat, correlate and contextualize relevant data, and take action? For most organizations, the honest answer is still measured in hours or days. Mature organizations are actively working toward reducing that time to minutes, and the most innovative teams are moving to sub-minute timescales using agentic AI.

The reality is that attackers don’t wait. Researchers across the industry, like the Sysdig Threat Research Team, have continuously shown that cloud attacks unfold in 10 minutes or less, and with AI and agentic workflows, the window for defense continues to shrink.

In mid-July 2026, Hugging Face disclosed a security incident unlike anything the industry had documented before. An agentic security research harness breached their production infrastructure. This harness was later confirmed to be part of OpenAI’s internal cyber-capability evaluation. Hugging Face logged more than 17,000 recorded events before the agents were contained, and they deployed LLM-driven analysis agents to reconstruct the timeline, extract indicators of compromise, and map the credentials touched. It took an AI to catch an AI.

Just one month prior, the Sysdig TRT documented JADEPUFFER, which targeted AI and ML infrastructure with purpose-built ransomware. The attacker was also an agent with no human at the keyboard.

These are not isolated incidents; they are the new normal. AI-assisted attacks have compressed the kill chain, and frontier AI models like Anthropic’s Claude Mythos have uncovered thousands of new vulnerabilities, too. It used to take attackers days to conduct reconnaissance, lateral movement, and exploitation, but now it only requires a few minutes.

“Cloud threats aren’t just fast; they are automated. Without real-time visibility, an attacker can move from a container escape to resource hijacking in minutes, spiking your compute costs before your team even receives an alert. Early detection is the only way to intercept execution before it impacts your bottom line.” — CISO at a Cryptocurrency Exchange and Trading Platform

The 555 Benchmark was designed for this

The 555 Benchmark for Cloud Detection and Response gives organizations a framework to meet this reality: detect threats in 5 seconds, investigate them in 5 minutes, and respond with precision in 5 minutes. And with agentic capabilities in the hands of defenders, meeting that benchmark is more than achievable.

When 555 was first introduced, it was a challenge; something to work toward. The Hugging Face incident, and other reports of agentic threat actors (ATAs), make clear why this benchmark is now a business imperative. When an autonomous system can break out and breach a production infrastructure via the fastest path, our concern is no longer whether AI can find vulnerabilities. It is whether organizations have continuous visibility into what attackers can reach, what they did, and how quickly they can be stopped. That is exactly what 555 operationalizes.

Ultimately, the 555 Benchmark isn’t a product or quick fix to implement, but a call to action to pressure-test your security processes against the speed of modern attacks. By continuously improving and modernizing your people, processes, and tooling, and by supplementing them with well-governed agentic AI security capabilities, you can reduce the risk of material breach, reputational damage, and financial loss.

Long gone are the days of working to defend your environment over the course of several days. Today, you only have minutes to respond to an attack.

“I don't want to know 15 minutes after someone breached my system. I need to know instantly so we can shut it down before the blast radius expands. To move at the necessary speed, you need to not only be alerted to the right things, but also respond appropriately. Having a benchmark gives us a goal to hold ourselves to.” — Désiré Banse, Former NIST Researcher and Security Operations Manager at a healthcare technology company

Introducing the updated 555 Benchmark Guides for CISOs and practitioners

To help organizations operationalize this framework for the AI era, Sysdig has republished two guides — aimed at different roles working toward the same goal — to support and encourage organizations in striving for 10-minute threat detection and response.

One guide is designed for the practitioners who work in and around the SOC: the security professionals in the trenches and on the front lines. The Hugging Face response team is a model for what this looks like in practice: After the breach was contained, they used agentic AI to do in hours what would’ve taken a team of analysts days. This guide focuses on how to operate at machine speed using the automation, AI tooling, and agentic workflows that make 555 achievable.

“Cloud threat detection and response goes far beyond tooling. You need to implement a specific set of skills and finesse and a different kind of mindset to detect cloud attacks in real time. ”

The Guide to the 555 Benchmark for Cloud Security Practitioners

The other guide is for the CISOs and security leaders who are responsible for leading teams through battle. They own the security strategy and risk, and must report value and breach impact to the board and to other business functions. This guide aligns security outcomes with organizational risk and reflects how, in the AI era, speed is the defining risk factor and defining board-level question.

“For large enterprises, a single hour of downtime costs over $100,000, with industries like finance, healthcare, media, and communications reaching well over $5 million per hour.”

The Guide to the 555 Benchmark for CISOs

Together, these guides provide a framework for security teams and leaders to meet common goals and expectations. It also helps them speak a unified language. By collaborating and following the strategies outlined, they can implement changes that modernize and accelerate cloud security practices, turning what were once ambitious goals into operational reality.

Enterprise security is like a symphony orchestra, with the CISO as the conductor. An oboist cannot sit in for a violinist, and different teams play their own distinct roles. SOC analysts, developers, platform engineers, and business stakeholders each contribute unique skills to the overall composition. Today, AI agents have joined that orchestra — not replacing whole sections, but playing alongside them, automating manual, repetitive processes and handling the parts that move too fast for humans hands alone, so humans can exercise judgment and have a greater impact. Synchronization and speed are survival requirements to maintain a secure and harmonious organization.

What you’ll learn

The updated 555 guides were designed to help organizations mature and modernize detection and response for the AI era through:

Collaboration: Working cross-functionally inside and outside of security and technical teams around shared context and outcomes to enable coordinated, real-time detection and response as humans and automated systems work together.

Integration: Unifying cloud-native telemetry and identity behaviors across cloud, SaaS, and AI systems to build real-time, decision-ready context across your entire environment to enable faster, more accurate detection and response.

Automation: Reducing manual effort across detection, investigation, and response to keep pace with AI-driven attacks by enabling orchestration to execute at machine speed.

Fast and automated incident response = Less attack risk = Lower chance of materiality = Business and operational value of security

If your organization operates in the cloud, now is the time to reassess how fast your security processes actually move. You don’t always need more tools or budget, but you do need the right architecture and better orchestration of the people, processes, and tooling you already have to modernize your cloud threat detection and response and meet the speed that threats demand.

Read and share The Guide to the 555 Benchmark for CISOs and The Guide to the 555 Benchmark for Cloud Security Practitioners today. Attackers are already running at machine speed — it’s time your defense does, too.

A critical Android flaw could allow an attacker to run code on a phone without any user action remotely, Google said in its November security bulletin.

The flaw, CVE-2026-58868, affects Android 14 through 17. Phones get the fix with security patch level 2026-11-01 or later, which phone makers and carriers send on their own schedules.

As of November 4, Google's bulletin did not report any attacks exploiting its flaws. None of them was in the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, kept by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, as of its November 3 update.

The flaw is a possible out-of-bounds write caused by a heap buffer overflow in the onOutputReceived function of the file FrameDecoder.cpp. Neither the bulletin nor the flaw's CVE record says how an attacker would reach that code.

Google's Critical rating assumes that the protections built into Android and Google's services are turned off or bypassed.

Older versions, such as Android 12 and 13, are not listed as affected by the flaw. Google's records do not say whether they contain it.

How to Check Your Phone

Google's help page gives these steps:

Open the Settings app.

Tap About phone, or About tablet, then Android version.

Find the dates for the Android security update and the Google Play system update.

The Android security update date is the phone's security patch level. A date of 2026-11-01 or later covers CVE-2026-58868 and the other flaws in the Framework, System, and Android runtime components.

A date of 2026-11-05 or later covers every flaw in the November bulletin, including those in the kernel and in parts from Arm, Imagination Technologies, MediaTek, Unisoc and Qualcomm.

Google sets two dates so phone makers can ship a set of fixes common to all Android devices sooner. It encourages them to include every fix in the bulletin.

Phones running Android 10 or later may also receive some fixes through Google Play system updates. This month's list for those updates includes another Critical flaw, CVE-2026-58876.

CVE-2026-58868 is not on that list, so the date to check for it is the Android security update.

The bulletin gives no workaround for phones that cannot install the update yet.

A Remote Denial-of-Service Flaw in Android's Text-Message Code

Another Critical flaw, CVE-2026-58882, could allow a remote denial-of-service attack with no user interaction, according to its CVE record. It is in decodeWapPdu, a function in Android's code for WAP Push messages that arrive via SMS.

On October 29, a researcher who publishes as Mark B posted a write-up called "SMS of Death" about a bug in the same function. Neither the bulletin nor the CVE record says whether CVE-2026-58882 is that bug.

One malformed WAP Push message crashes com.android.phone and ends any active call, including emergency calls, according to the write-up. In tests on several phone models, the crash happened every time.

The attacker needs only the target's phone number, and the message never shows up in the inbox. The phone retries the message each time it starts, so it can crash on startup until the message is removed.

A proof-of-concept app that sends such a message from one phone to another is public. Phones running Android 12 and 13 run the same code but do not receive the fix that newer versions do, the researcher says.

Other Critical Flaws

Google's November bulletin lists 216 vulnerabilities, 23 of them rated Critical. Two more Critical flaws could allow remote code execution: CVE-2026-58876 and CVE-2026-58936, both in Android's System component.

Six Critical flaws are in the kernel, two of them in Bluetooth code. The most severe kernel flaw could allow a remote attacker to gain elevated privileges without user interaction.

The 2026-11-05 patch level also fixes Critical flaws in MediaTek modem code and in a closed-source Qualcomm component. In its November bulletin, MediaTek describes its Critical modem flaws as out-of-bounds writes and says it is not aware of any active exploitation.

France's national blood service has confirmed that a cyberattack targeting a refrigeration equipment provider raised temperature and defrost settings at three of its facilities, threatening stored blood products.

The French Blood Establishment (Établissement français du sang or EFS), which manages blood collection, processing, and distribution across France, said the incident occurred on November 2 and affected systems used to monitor and control cold-storage chambers.

According to a statement published on November 3, EFS was not directly targeted in the cyberattack, but was instead its refrigeration supplier.

While EFS has not named the affected supplier, European refrigeration equipment provider Coolworld Rentals confirmed in a statement that a cybersecurity incident involving remote monitoring software had affected a limited number of its refrigeration units.

Coolworld says the attackers exploited a vulnerability in a third-party component, which was outside the company's direct control.

"The vulnerability currently being reported in the media relates to a component from a third-party supplier and was outside Coolworld's direct control," the company said.

"Only a limited number of Coolworld units were affected, and Coolworld responded promptly and took appropriate measures."

The company said it is working with affected customers but will not comment on individual cases.

At EFS, the incident raised temperature and defrost thresholds in affected cold-storage chambers to extremely high levels.

These facilities store blood products before they are distributed to hospitals, as well as biological samples maintained by the EFS.

EFS says its monitoring and alarm systems quickly detected the temperature change, allowing staff to fix impacted equipment or transfer products to other refrigeration facilities.

"No health impact has been identified, and no loss of blood products has been reported," EFS said in its statement [translated from French].

The organization confirmed that plasma bags intended for transfusions and plasma used to manufacture medicines were either transferred or secured, preventing damage to the products.

Blood collection and distribution operations have continued without interruption.

EFS says its technical teams are working with France's national cybersecurity agency (ANSSI) and the Ministry of Health, and it has strengthened monitoring of refrigeration equipment and temperatures.

The incident follows a wave of cyberattacks targeting refrigeration systems across Europe, where attackers remotely manipulate temperature settings or activate defrost functions that turn off cooling.

In October, cyberattacks disrupted refrigeration systems at an estimated 250 to 350 French supermarkets, including Intermarché, Carrefour Market, Monoprix, Leclerc, and Super U.

In those attacks, hackers reportedly compromised refrigeration controllers running older Danfoss software and remotely activated automatic defrosting functions, raising temperatures and forcing stores to discard fresh and frozen products.

These attacks targeted Danfoss AK-SM/AK-SC and Copeland/Dixell XWEB refrigeration controllers, which are used to monitor and manage cooling equipment remotely.

A second wave of attacks occurred this month, affecting more than 115 stores across Belgium, the Netherlands, Sweden, Luxembourg, Ireland, and Estonia.

Some refrigeration systems were shut down entirely, while others had their temperature settings changed remotely.

At one Swedish supermarket, the system reportedly began generating heat, while another store reported that temperatures were changed to 50°C (122°F).

Belgian refrigeration company Sabcobel previously said that attackers behind the November incidents exploited the same vulnerability used in October's attacks against French supermarkets.

In 2025, the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) disclosed two vulnerabilities affecting Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA controllers, tracked as CVE-2025-41450 and CVE-2025-41451.

The flaws could allow attackers to bypass authentication and execute commands remotely on vulnerable systems, potentially giving them control over refrigeration equipment.

However, it has not been confirmed whether these vulnerabilities are being exploited in the attacks.

b982e467e453.text:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has added a security flaw in WordPress Core to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, citing evidence of active exploitation.

The high-severity vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-119977 (CVSS score: 8.1), is a case of Time-of-check Time-of-use (TOCTOU) race condition that could be exploited to achieve arbitrary code execution on affected servers. Patches for the flaw were released late last month.

"WordPress Core contains a time-of-check time-of-use (TOCTOU) race condition vulnerability that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code on the server during the upgrade window," CISA said. "This is due to predictable, web-accessible staging paths used during full-package core upgrades."

Details of the flaw emerged last week when Wordfence said exploiting the vulnerability does not require an account on the site. That said, it does require an attacker to exploit a brief window during a complete Core update that could allow unauthenticated code execution.

During the first 21 hours after public disclosure, the WordPress security company said it recorded more than 18,500 requests targeting staged "setup-config.php" installer paths. As of writing, 12,632 attacks attempting to exploit the flaw have been blocked in the last 24 hours.

Telemetry data from Previdian shows that three exploitation attempts have been recorded against its honeypot censors from an IP address geolocated in the U.K. The exploitation events were observed on October 30, 2026.

With exploitation now officially confirmed by CISA, Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies have time until November 6, 2026, to apply the fixes.

1be6e03d1804.text:
Cybersecurity researchers have discovered a new Windows infostealer malware called VOLTA-AUTODOXER (aka VOLTA) that makes use of a large language model (LLM) to rank a victim's stolen data by their monetization value.

Like other typical stealer families, VOLTA is equipped to harvest passwords and cookies from Chromium-based web browsers; data from Outlook profiles and Slack workspaces; payment cards; cryptocurrency wallet seed phrases; Discord, Telegram, Steam, and Roblox sessions; Microsoft OAuth tokens; SSH and cloud-provider keys; Wi-Fi profiles; and screenshots.

"VOLTA builds a structured evidence bundle about the person behind the machine," Cisco Talos researcher Ryan Fetterman said. "This bundle contains geolocation and home address, employer and employer domain, inferred birth year, card last-4 digits, Slack workspaces, document authorship metadata, iPhone backup indicators, and a live Roblox account valuation."

To make this information more valuable, the malware uses stolen session access to search the victim's Gmail account for receipts to corroborate the home address by extracting emails related to Amazon, DoorDash, Uber Eats, Grubhub, Walmart, and PayPal.

Once the necessary information is collected, the bundle is serialized and fed into an artificial intelligence (AI) system for analysis using OpenRouter, a unified LLM API gateway and routing service, along with a system prompt. The requests are defaulted to Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.6, failing which it falls back to Moonshot AI's Kimi K2 and Google's Gemini 2.5 Flash.

"VOLTA uses a multi-model architecture to fall back resiliently if it hits a model's refusal, checking each response for phrases like 'I can't' or 'I'm not able,' before passing on to a chain of up to three models," Talos said.

VOLTA features a 240-word system prompt that instructs the model to assume the role of a "forensic intelligence analyst" responsible for drafting a target assessment based on data from a structured evidence bundle. "The bundle is the ONLY permissible source of facts; your training knowledge must never supply a fact about the subject," reads a line from the prompt.

"The required output includes a section titled 'WHAT THEY'RE WORTH' with valuables ranked by monetization with a low/medium/high tier, and a section on 'THEIR OPSEC' containing an assessment of the victim's security posture and password hygiene," Talos explained.

"The model is the operator's triage analyst; it turns a raw credential log into a prioritized and citation-backed dossier of the victim and their monetizable assets."

Data exfiltration happens over Telegram at three different stages -

Right after the stealer runs, containing details about browser passwords, cookies, payment cards, cryptocurrency wallets; Discord, Steam, and Roblox tokens; Wi-Fi passwords, and screenshots

After the AI call, which includes the captured data and the results of the LLM analysis

After the live enrichment step, which includes Gmail receipts and order histories

What's more, VOLTA makes use of a template containing six slots that are filled in at build time. This includes the Telegram channel used for data exfiltration, API keys, and other settings.

This approach suggests that the malware author is likely either advertising a builder kit to prospective customers or operating it as a bespoke tool under their control to compile a custom binary for each order.

"If VOLTA is indeed a commoditized malware, then the AI dossier capability isn't something the author invented for their own operations," Talos said. "It is a feature which enables a customer of any level of sophistication to point it at victims and start receiving ranked target assessments in their Telegram inbox."

"VOLTA is a mature stealer with a late-stage AI layer added for one purpose: relieving the operator of analytical work. The axis of AI improvement here is not speed or scale but effort displacement."

The disclosure comes as adversarial adoption of generative AI (aka GenAI) is quickly becoming the new normal, as threat actors incorporate the technology into their workflows to develop custom tools or find valuable data, thereby increasing the likelihood of success of their attacks.

"GenAI technologies are also well suited to examine massive amounts of data for the purposes of classification or content searching," Zscaler ThreatLabz said. "Once an attacker has access to the victim’s system, GenAI can therefore be used to search all materials to which a victim's system has access, seeking the most valuable or sensitive data for theft or encryption during the next phase of the attack."

A ransomware actor can leverage this method to identify and acquire the most sensitive data from a compromised network, maximizing the chances that the victim will pay up.

Last week, Talos also detailed an AI-enabled framework called NIK C2 that gives attackers remote access, credential theft, keylogging, defense evasion, surveillance, and ransomware capabilities, while integrating an OpenAI client to send stolen data for AI analysis within the compromised session.

A Go-based, Windows remote access tool, NIK C2 grants persistent control over compromised hosts and supports over 52 commands sent by a command-and-control (C2) server to collect a wide range of data.

The OpenAI integration is notable for the fact that the threat actor can abuse a victim's own OpenAI API key to execute the AI-driven analysis. Specifically, the plant checks if the actor has supplied an API key. In the absence of one, it scans the victim's environment variables for the string "OPENAI_API_KEY" and uses it.

This is a form of LLMjacking, where bad actors steal access to another party's AI model to run their own operations – in this case, against the victim itself – while the legitimate owner pays for the computing power. In addition, it allows the attacker to evade detection by obscuring who made the requests.

"This fallback is not a backup mechanism for API key resolution. It is a deliberate design with significant operational implications," Talos said. "If the victim has configured an OpenAI account on their machine, that account's API key will be used to fund the actor's AI inference."

"NIK C2 reshapes adversary tradecraft by collapsing collection and exploitation into a single continuous session, effectively erasing the offline processing delays that historically granted defenders critical detection windows," Talos said.

ad9ac4b6d645.text:
North Korea was behind the theft of more than $6bn from cryptocurrency exchange Binance last week, according to the FBI.

A brief statement from the Bureau published on October 31 attributed the breach to the TraderTraitor group (aka Jade Sleet, UNC4899, Slow Pisces).

“The FBI, together with partners at the US Secret Service and the Internal Revenue Service Criminal Investigation (IRS-CI), has observed TraderTraitor actors converting stolen assets primarily into Ethereum (ETH),” it read.

“It is expected these assets will then be further laundered by converting them using decentralized finance products (DeFi) and instant swap services as they prepare them for further laundering stages.”

Read more on TraderTraitor: US and Japan Blame North Korea for $308m Crypto Heist.

The FBI and its partners urged crypto entities including THORNode operators, RPC node operators, instant exchanges, DeFi services, blockchain analytics firms and other virtual asset service providers to “block transactions with or derived from addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder these stolen assets.”

According to Blockchain analytics company Elliptic, around $2.9bn of the stolen funds have been frozen or seized, but that still leaves almost $3.3bn outside the reach of issuers.

“At current prices, the attacker now controls around $3.25bn of assets that cannot be frozen by an issuer, spread across more than 800 addresses. This includes around 584,000 ETH ($1.32bn), 18,327 BTC ($1.42bn) and 233 million XRP,” Elliptic explained.

“The ETH includes TRX laundered through bridges, which arrives on Ethereum and is split across hundreds of fresh wallets. Almost all of the stolen TRX has now been laundered. The XRP, SOL and NEAR, worth around $439m, have not moved at all since they were stolen.”

Binance Investigation Continues

Binance has said it will cover the costs of the incident, so customer funds are not in danger. However, it continues to investigate the actual cause of the breach.

Originally, the firm claimed that a compromised DevOps laptop may have been the source of the incident, but later added that it “uncovered additional points of breach” in what it is describing as a “complex attack.”

The attack was carried out by more than one individual, and used a “self-destruct mechanism that destroyed tooling and traces as it ran,” which has made forensic analysis harder, according to Elliptic.

TraderTraitor, which also has links to the Lazarus Group, APT 38 and AppleJeus, has been pegged for a string of historic crypto heists.

These include attacks on Japanese firm DMM, which cost the firm $308m, as well as Alphapo ($60m), CoinsPaid ($37m) and Atomic Wallet ($100m). TraderTraitor was also blamed for the previous record setter for biggest ever crypto breach, when it stole $1.5bn from Bybit.
